title: India's approach progressively shifting from Post- Disaster Relief to Disaster Prevention in Landslide Management: Dr. Jitendra Singh at 7th World Landslide Forum
subtitle:
“India’s landslide susceptibility mapping completed across 4.3 lakh sq km; inventory of nearly 91,000 historical landslides compiled”

National Landslide Forecasting Centre established in Kolkata extends forecasting activities to 20 districts, says Dr. Jitendra Singh

₹1,000 crore National Landslide Mitigation Project approved for 15 states; ₹1,115.67 crore sanctioned for disaster mitigation and capacity building: Dr. Jitendra Singh

AI-based prediction, geospatial technologies, satellite monitoring and last-mile early warning to strengthen landslide resilience: Dr. Jitendra Singh
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                23 NOV 2026 4:25PM by PIB Delhi
content:
Union Minister of State (Independent Charge) for Science & Technology and Earth Sciences, and MoS in the PMO, Dr. Jitendra Singh, today said India's approach is progressively shifting its approach to landslide management from post-disaster relief to prevention, preparedness and risk reduction, marking a major transformation in the country's disaster management strategy.
Addressing the inaugural session of the 7th World Landslide Forum (WLF7) at Amrita Vishwa Vidyapeetham, Faridabad, the Minister said India is moving away from waiting for disasters to occur and mobilising relief machinery afterwards, towards anticipating risks, strengthening early warning systems and preventing avoidable loss of lives and infrastructure.
The 7th World Landslide Forum, being held from November 22 to 27, 2026, is being hosted in India for the first time by Amrita Vishwa Vidyapeetham in collaboration with the International Consortium on Landslides (ICL) and the International Programme on Landslides (IPL). The inaugural session brought together international experts, scientists and policymakers from more than 75 countries.
Dignitaries present included Secretary, Ministry of Earth Sciences, Dr. Srinivas Kumar Tummala; Chancellor of Amrita Vishwa Vidyapeetham, Mata Amritanandamayi Devi; Vice-Chancellor Dr. Vikram Rangan; Pro-Vice-Chancellor Dr. Maneesha Vinodini Ramesh; and other academic leaders and international delegates.
Dr. Jitendra Singh said India's diverse geological and geophysical landscape, encompassing the Himalayas, Western Ghats, northeastern region and other vulnerable mountain areas, makes landslide risk reduction a critical national priority. Recalling major landslide disasters in Wayanad, Kerala, Chamoli in Uttarakhand, Sikkim, Himachal Pradesh and Jammu and Kashmir, he stressed the need for interdisciplinary research, continuous monitoring and coordinated scientific efforts to minimise the impact of such disasters.
The Minister said the Department of Science and Technology has been engaged in geospatial technologies and natural resource data management since 1982 through the Natural Resources Data Management System (NRDMS). The National Geospatial Policy and National Geospatial Programme introduced in 2019 have further strengthened India's geospatial ecosystem by leveraging contemporary technologies. The Department has supported landslide warning and early detection systems, low-cost AI-based and video-based monitoring solutions, geological and geophysical investigations, vulnerability mapping and related research initiatives.
Dr. Jitendra Singh said national landslide susceptibility mapping has been completed across approximately 4.3 lakh square kilometres, while the landslide inventory database has compiled information on nearly 91,000 historical landslides by the end of 2025. The National Landslide Forecasting Centre was established in Kolkata in 2024, while the Regional Landslide Forecasting System, established in 2020, is supporting experimental and operational forecasting across vulnerable regions. The National Landslide Forecasting Centre has now extended its activities to 20 districts.
The Minister said a high-level committee headed by the union home minister has recently approved ₹1,115.67 crore for disaster mitigation and capacity-building exercises, along with ₹1,000 crore for the National Landslide Mitigation Project covering 15 states, including 10 Himalayan states and five other landslide-vulnerable states. He also referred to institutional collaborations and scientific partnerships involving the Geological Survey of India, National Centre for Medium Range Weather Forecasting and Wadia Institute of Himalayan Geology, Dehradun, which are advancing geological investigations, hazard assessment, integrated monitoring, satellite-based observations and AI-enabled landslide mapping and prediction.
Highlighting the role of weather science in landslide risk management, Dr. Jitendra Singh said Mission Mausam, launched with an initial allocation of ₹2,000 crore, is strengthening India's weather observation, forecasting and modelling capabilities. The Bharat Forecast System, introduced in 2025, provides weather forecasts at a spatial resolution of up to approximately six kilometres, enabling more localised information for disaster preparedness, administration and infrastructure planning.
The Minister stressed that rainfall forecasts alone cannot adequately predict landslides, as scientific assessment must also account for geology, soil moisture, pore-water pressure, slope deformation and ground stability. He called for closer integration of weather forecasts with geological, geotechnical, hydrological and real-time ground observations to develop more accurate, actionable and location-specific landslide early warning systems.
Dr. Jitendra Singh appreciated Amrita Vishwa Vidyapeetham's contribution to landslide research and early warning technologies, particularly its wireless sensor network-based landslide detection system deployed in Munnar, Kerala. Developed through sustained indigenous research and supported by the Department of Science and Technology, the system combines real-time measurements of rainfall, soil moisture, pore-water pressure and other geophysical parameters to assess changing slope conditions.
He also referred to the advanced landslide early warning system deployed in Sikkim with support and co-funding from the Ministry of Earth Sciences, in collaboration with the Sikkim State Disaster Management Authority, as an example of government-supported university research translating into field-level applications. The Minister said such initiatives reflect the importance of indigenous innovation, Make in India and Atmanirbhar Bharat in developing technologies with direct societal relevance.
Dr. Jitendra Singh called for strengthening integrated geospatial databases, satellite and sensor-based monitoring, institutional collaboration and the translation of scientific advancements into effective last-mile warnings. He said the future of landslide risk reduction lies in combining artificial intelligence, geospatial science, satellite observations, ground sensors and interdisciplinary research with practical implementation, so that scientific knowledge reaches vulnerable communities in time to protect lives, infrastructure and livelihoods.
The Minister expressed hope that the 7th World Landslide Forum would advance global scientific collaboration, technology transfer, institutional capacity-building and impact-based early warning systems, while translating scientific deliberations into practical pathways for safer slopes, resilient infrastructure and disaster-resilient communities.

Further, Shri Yadav congratulated the awardees selected during the Wildlife Week, and highlighted that the frontline staff and local communities are the backbone of India's wildlife conservation efforts. The Minister then felicitated them for exemplary wildlife conservation work:
Frontline Staff – Protection and Anti-Poaching:

Frontline Staff – Wildlife Monitoring and Special Skills:
Shri Umesh Bharat Kalsarpe (Maharashtra), Shri AshwinsinhKiritsinhJadeja (Gujarat) and the Bahraich Human-Wildlife Conflict Management Group (Uttar Pradesh).

Shree MahavirMachchhimarSahakariMandali Ltd., Mangrol (Gujarat), for whale shark conservation, and Ponnuruvi Eco-Tourism Management Committee, Sirumalai Hills (Tamil Nadu).

‘marine conservation’.

-
Management Effectiveness Evaluation (MEE) of Coastal and Marine Protected Areas; Pan-India Assessment and Monitoring of Marine Turtles; Milestones of Recovery of Dugongs and their Habitats in India (2016–2026); and
,
Mitigating the Impacts of Linear Infrastructure on Wildlife.
These presentations highlighted the status and achievements in conservation of wildlife, especially related to the management effectiveness of marine protected areas, marine turtle and dugongs. The presentation of mitigation of linear infrastructure on wildlife highlighted on addressing the challenges on consequential impact on wildlife and the need for empowering a wide range of stakeholders, including infrastructure planners, builders, environmental consultants, wildlife managers, regulators, policymakers, and analysts.
In line with the theme of marine wildlife conservation, several
publications
were released during the meeting, that highlight the Ministry’s conservation initiatives relating to marine biodiversity conservation. These include:
Management Effectiveness Evaluation (MEE) of Coastal and Marine Protected Areas:
Presents the findings of the 2024–26 assessment covering 108 coastal and marine Protected Areas, highlighting management performance, best practices and priority areas for strengthening conservation.
Pan-India Assessment and Monitoring of Marine Turtles:
Undertaken by the Wildlife Institute of India (WII) under the Ministry’s Development of Wildlife Habitats scheme, the assessment covers three nesting seasons (2022–25), approximately 1,300 km of coastline and 360 beach stretches, providing insights into the nesting status of four marine turtle species.
Milestones of Recovery of Dugongs and their Habitats in India (2016–2026):
Documents a decade of conservation efforts under the CAMPA-funded programme implemented by WII, including the first drone-based dugong population estimate in Tamil Nadu (270 ± 16), identification of seagrass habitats and notification of India’s first Dugong Conservation Reserve in Palk Bay.
Status of Arabian Sea Humpback Whale in India:
Presents the findings of WII’s 2022–25 assessment, identifying seven potential sighting hotspots and highlighting threats, particularly entanglement in fishing gear, to guide future conservation interventions.
Marine Turtle Knowledge Products:
Three publications—
Technical Protocol of Marking Marine Turtles
,
Tracking Marine Turtles in Indian Waters
and
Marine Turtles of India

the

a
document pertaining to small cat conservation

c
overs nine species of small cats found in India and provides practical guidance on species identification, field surveys and monitoring. National HPV Vaccination Campaign: Progress and Coverage
Launched by Hon’ble Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi in February 2026, the National HPV Vaccination Campaign provides free, safe and voluntary single-dose HPV vaccination, with parental consent, to 14-year-old girls at designated Government health facilities
. In less than nine months, over 1 crore doses have been administered, achieving nearly 87% coverage of the annual target cohort of approximately 1.2 crore girls.
State-wise Progress in HPV Vaccination
Six States — Gujarat, Uttar Pradesh, Andhra Pradesh, Mizoram, Madhya Pradesh and Bihar — have achieved 100% coverage of their identified target populations. Twelve States have crossed 80% coverage.
Assam has recorded 95.63% coverage, Telangana 95.28%, Karnataka 93.16%, Uttarakhand 90.17%, Chhattisgarh 86.21% and Rajasthan 85.23%. Kerala has recorded 77.02%, Tamil Nadu 76.12% and Odisha 74.90%. The Union Territory of Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu has recorded 72.99%.
In terms of the number of girls vaccinated, Uttar Pradesh leads with over 29.33 lakh, followed by Bihar with over 13.70 lakh and Gujarat with over 7.75 lakh. States have adopted locally tailored approaches to extend vaccination services across rural, urban, remote and geographically challenging areas. State-led initiatives in Bihar, Tamil Nadu and Sikkim have also been integrated with the national campaign.
Centre-State Coordination and Community Engagement
The campaign is being implemented through coordination between the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, State and Union Territory Governments, district administrations and healthcare teams. Paediatricians, gynaecologists and specialists from premier medical institutions such as AIIMS have supported awareness efforts through credible, science-based information. Teachers, Accredited Social Health Activists (ASHAs), Auxiliary Nurse Midwives (ANMs) and other frontline workers have engaged with parents and communities to address concerns and encourage informed participation.
U-WIN Supports Digital Monitoring and Access to Vaccination
The U-WIN platform enables real-time monitoring, beneficiary tracking and digital vaccination records. It helps programme managers monitor district-level progress, identify coverage gaps and eligible girls yet to be vaccinated, and support planning and resource allocation. Parents can also use the platform to book HPV vaccination slots for their daughters and download digital vaccination certificates.
HPV Vaccination: An Important Preventive Intervention Against Cervical Cancer
Persistent infection with certain high-risk types of Human Papillomavirus is responsible for the vast majority of cervical cancer cases. HPV vaccination is among the most effective preventive interventions against such infections. More than 800 million HPV vaccine doses have been administered worldwide, while nearly two decades of research and real-world experience demonstrate strong protection against vaccine-targeted HPV infections and associated precancerous conditions. Vaccination at the age of 14 years aims to provide protection well before potential exposure to HPV.
Beneficiary Safety Remains a Central Priority
Vaccination sessions are conducted at designated Government health facilities under the direct supervision of trained Medical Officers. Sites are linked to 24×7 healthcare centres for prompt assessment, monitoring and management of any rare Adverse Events Following Immunization (AEFI). Established safety protocols, trained personnel and appropriate medical arrangements support the safe conduct of vaccination sessions. The Ministry continues to emphasise transparent communication, scientific evidence and informed parental consent.
Sustaining Momentum Towards Reaching Every Eligible Girl
The Ministry of Health and Family Welfare will continue working with State Governments, district administrations, medical professionals, frontline healthcare workers, educational institutions and communities to address coverage gaps and reach all eligible girls. Parents and guardians can visit their nearest designated Government health facility or access the U-WIN platform for information and vaccination slot booking.
The achievement of administering over 1 crore HPV vaccine doses in less than nine months marks important progress in India's efforts to protect adolescent girls against cervical cancer. The National HPV Vaccination Campaign reflects the Government's continued commitment to strengthening preventive healthcare and ensuring that every eligible girl has access to this vital protection.

title: ICMR’s SAMPADA survey shows lower prevalence of anaemia compared to previous national surveys
subtitle:
Severe anaemia below 2% across most age groups, with the majority of cases being mild

SAMPADA provides comprehensive national evidence to further strengthen Anaemia Mukt Bharat

SAMPADA uses gold standard method of venous blood sampling and automated analysers for haemoglobin estimation

One of the world’s largest nutrition surveys, covering over 2 lakh individuals across 183 districts in 35 States and Union Territories
ministry: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                23 NOV 2026 6:35PM by PIB Delhi
content:
The Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR), Department of Health Research, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare has released key findings from the Survey for Assessment of Markers of Population Health, Activity, Diet and Anthropometry (SAMPADA) 2023-2025, providing comprehensive national evidence on anaemia and micronutrient deficiencies across the life course.
SAMPADA represents
one of the largest and most comprehensive nutrition surveys undertaken globally
. The survey covered more than 2 lakh individuals from over 81,000 households across 183 districts in 35 States and Union Territories. More than 1.7 lakh blood samples were analysed for haemoglobin estimation across different age, sex and physiological groups.
A major strength of SAMPADA is the use of
gold standard method of venous blood sampling and automated analysers for haemoglobin estimation
, providing greater accuracy and reproducibility. In a sub-sample, the survey also assessed iron status, folate, vitamin B12, together with inflammatory biomarkers C-reactive protein (CRP) and alpha-1-acid glycoprotein (AGP) to obtain national level prevalence estimates.
The SAMPADA findings show an encouraging shift with
overall lower prevalence of anaemia
compared to previous surveys. The difference is particularly large in case of  children aged 12-59 months who had 42% anaemia prevalence. Adolescent girls aged 10-19 years had anaemia prevalence of 46%, adolescent boys aged 10-19 years and men aged 20–59 years had 22-23% anaemia prevalence whereas women of reproductive age had 56% prevalence.
The survey also provides nationally representative estimates among older adults, extending the assessment of anaemia to an age group for which national-level evidence has been limited. The findings also highlight important differences by age, sex, physiological status and location, reinforcing the need for population-specific approaches rather than a single strategy for all groups.
The key highlights of the report are:
Majority of anaemia is mild, highlighting opportunities for early action.
Mild anaemia constitutes a substantial proportion of the overall anaemia burden. About half of anaemic women including pregnant and lactating women, adolescent girls and children, have mild anaemia indicating considerably lower risk of serious health consequences than moderate or severe anaemia. Anaemia prevalence is much lower among adolescent boys, adult and older men and even among those affected, three-fourths have only mild anaemia.
Severe anaemia was observed in less than 2% people in majority of the age groups
.
Iron deficiency accounts for about half of the anaemia cases in women, adolescent girls and children.
The micronutrient assessment shows that although iron deficiency is the predominant contributor to anaemia in vulnerable population groups, it accounts for about half of the overall anaemia burden highlighting the need to simultaneously address multiple nutritional and non-nutritional causes of anaemia including infections, hemoglobinopathies, as well as inflammation related to chronic disease. However, the
p
revalence of vitamin B12 and folate deficiency was similar in both anaemic and non-anaemic individuals across population groups, indicating limited contribution of these micronutrient deficiencies to anaemia in India.
Iron deficiency is concentrated in specific life-stages and in moderate and severe cases of anaemia.
SAMPADA findings show that iron deficiency is largely restricted to population groups including under five children, adolescent girls and women of reproductive age while adolescent boys, men and the elderly have low prevalence of iron deficiency. Importantly, people with moderate and severe anaemia have a high prevalence of iron deficiency and need to be identified by testing for appropriate treatment and tracking till resolution as envisaged in AMB 2.0
“
SAMPADA provides nationally representative estimates of anaemia across children, adolescents, adults, pregnant and lactating women and older adults, together with detailed information on micronutrient deficiencies to evaluate potential causes of anaemia. It is encouraging that prevalence of anaemia is lower in SAMPADA compared to previous national surveys. The comprehensive anaemia profiling in SAMPADA survey provides an evidence base to strengthen the ongoing national efforts towards Anaemia Mukt Bharat”, said Dr Rajiv Bahl, Secretary, Department of Health Research, Govt of India and DG, ICMR
“These findings support more targeted, population-specific and life-course approaches to anaemia prevention and management. The evidence can contribute, while also identifying areas where further research and improved surveillance are required” explained Dr Bharati Kulkarni, Director, ICMR-NIN
The details can be accessed from the link
https://www.nin.res.in/ebooks/Sampada_Anaemia_BM_Factsheet.pdf
.

title: Union Health Secretary Smt. Punya Salila Srivastava inaugurates India’s first dedicated Human Metabolic Chamber Facility at Christian Medical College (CMC) Vellore
subtitle:
Smt. Srivastava calls for robust, India-specific research to strengthen understanding of metabolic risks and inform preventive healthcare

Over 7.8 crore yoga sessions conducted at Ayushman Arogya Mandirs to promote healthier lifestyles and preventive healthcare: Union Health Secretary

Union Health Secretary highlights initiatives to take forward Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi's call for 10 per cent reduction in oil consumption, including Sugar and Oil Boards and 'Aaj Se Thoda Kam' campaign

Tata Institute of Fundamental Research (TIFR) and CMC Vellore collaborate to advance research on nutrition, diabetes, obesity and metabolic health
ministry: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                23 NOV 2026 4:23PM by PIB Delhi
content:
Union Health Secretary Smt. Punya Salila Srivastava today inaugurated India's first dedicated Human Metabolic Chamber Facility at Christian Medical College (CMC), Vellore. Established jointly by the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research (TIFR) and CMC Vellore, the facility will strengthen research into human metabolism, nutrition, diabetes, obesity and other metabolic conditions. The initiative is in line with the vision of Hon'ble Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi to strengthen prevention and healthcare for all, and create a Swasth and Viksit Bharat.
Addressing the gathering, Smt. Srivastava congratulated TIFR, the Advanced Research Unit on Metabolism, Development & Aging (ARUMDA) and CMC Vellore on the initiative and acknowledged the Department of Atomic Energy for supporting the collaboration. She underscored the importance of generating evidence that reflects the diversity and specific risk profiles of India's population, noting that findings from other countries may not adequately capture them.
The Human Metabolic Chamber is a room-sized calorimeter that measures oxygen consumption and carbon dioxide production while a volunteer lives, eats and sleeps inside for 24 hours or longer. The measurements help determine total energy expenditure and how the body uses fat and carbohydrates across meals, physical activity and sleep. The facility complements ARUMDA's National Analytical Facility for Nutrition and Metabolism Research, established last year, enabling researchers to link molecular and biochemical measurements with the body's energy utilisation.
The collaboration also draws on CMC Vellore's clinical expertise in diabetes and other endocrine and metabolic disorders, including its past studies on insulin sensitivity and energy expenditure in individuals with a history of undernutrition and low birth weight. The facility was set up with funding from the Department of Atomic Energy and Corporate Social Responsibility support from Hindustan Unilever Limited, with expert advice from NUTRIM at Maastricht University and network support from the Embassy of the Kingdom of the Netherlands in India.
Smt. Srivastava highlighted the Government's efforts to strengthen prevention under the Ayushman Bharat Yojana, with 1.87 lakh Ayushman Arogya Mandirs providing primary healthcare and population-based screening for non-communicable diseases and three types of cancers, including a community-based assessment of all individuals above 30 years of age. She said over 781 district NCD clinics and 6,489 NCD clinics at Community Health Centres ensure follow-up and continuum of care, and that the Rashtriya Bal Swasthya Karyakram (RBSK) 2.0 enables early identification of at-risk children. She added that five more diseases, including chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), stroke and chronic kidney disease (CKD), will also be covered under the National Programme for Non-communicable Diseases.
Taking forward the Hon'ble Prime Minister's call for a 10 per cent reduction in oil consumption, she noted, initiatives have been rolled out, including Sugar and Oil Boards, awareness interventions in schools, the 'Aaj Se Thoda Kam' campaign and outreach through social media, radio and videos. Yoga and wellness activities have also been integrated into services at the Mandirs, with over 7.8 crore cumulative yoga sessions conducted so far. She added that institutes such as ICMR-NIN are using technology to make healthy choices easier, including an AI-powered tool being developed to help consumers understand the nutritional value of packaged foods.
Underscoring institutional collaboration, Smt. Srivastava encouraged TIFR, ARUMDA and CMC Vellore to work with the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare and other national institutions on a focused research agenda addressing the country's health needs. She also pointed to the potential of the Pan-AIIMS Research Consortium, working with research facilities such as the Human Metabolic Chamber, to strengthen research capabilities and contribute to robust, evidence-based national datasets.
The programme was attended by Prof. Biju George, Director, CMC Vellore; Prof. Jayaram Chengalur, Director, TIFR; Prof. Ullas Kolthur, Director, BRIC-Centre for DNA Fingerprinting and Diagnostics; Prof. Mahendra Sonavane, ARUMDA-TIFR; Prof. Nihal Thomas, Head, Stem Cell Centre, CMC Vellore; Mr. Nico Schiettekatte, Health Counsellor, Embassy of the Kingdom of the Netherlands; representatives of Hindustan Unilever Limited; and Prof. Felix Jebasingh, Department of Endocrinology, Diabetes and Metabolism, CMC Vellore, among other faculty members and officials.

title: ‘Pagla Ghora’ and ‘Ohh My Dog’ Explore the Profound Dimensions of Human Conscience and Unconditional Love at 57th IFFI
subtitle:
Art Has No Borders, Only Roots: Sekhar Das on the Universal Appeal of ‘Pagla Ghora’

Animals Do Not Carry the Burden of Prejudice; Their Loyalty Is Absolute: Amit Rai, Director of ‘Ohh My Dog’
content:
Goa, 23 November 2026
While one story brings the ghosts of the past face to face with a restless conscience, the other celebrates a love so pure that no distance or adversity can diminish it. Exploring two contrasting yet deeply moving dimensions of the human experience, ‘
Pagla Ghora’
and ‘
Ohh My Dog’
, the Bengali and Hindi selections in the Indian Panorama, took centre stage at a press conference today at the 57th International Film Festival of India (IFFI) in Goa.
Filmmakers Sekhar Das and Amit Rai, accompanied by acclaimed Bengali actress Gargee RoyChowdhury and producer Dr. Prabir Bhaumik, interacted with the media, sharing insights into their respective films and their exploration of guilt, betrayal, empathy and unconditional devotion. Together, these narratives celebrate cinema's power to transcend linguistic and cultural boundaries through the universal language of human emotion.
Pagla Ghora
: A Haunting Journey into Guilt, Remorse and the Human Conscience
National Film Award-winning filmmaker Sekhar Das, along with lead actress Gargee RoyChowdhury and producer Dr. Prabir Bhaumik, shared insights into the cinematic adaptation of legendary playwright Badal Sircar’s post-realist theatrical masterpiece, ‘
Pagla Ghora’
. Set against the eerie backdrop of a forest crematorium at night, the film follows four men who gather for the cremation of a woman who died by suicide. As her spirit confronts them, their buried secrets surface, revealing a shared history of betrayal and infidelity. What unfolds is a haunting exploration of guilt, emotional abandonment and the human conscience, underscoring the painful truth that remorse often comes too late.
Speaking about the enduring relevance of Badal Sircar's work and the universal appeal of regional cinema, Director Sekhar Das underscored the power of authentic storytelling to transcend linguistic and geographical boundaries. "Art does not have any borders; it only has roots. When a story is deeply rooted in human conscience and emotional truth, it speaks to audiences everywhere, regardless of language," he remarked.
Gargee RoyChowdhury reflected on the emotional intricacies of portraying a character whose presence becomes both a mirror to human frailty and a catalyst for moral awakening. Her role, she highlighted, demanded a delicate engagement with the film's layered emotional landscape.
Producer Dr. Prabir Bhaumik emphasized the significance of supporting literary and theatrical adaptations, noting their vital contribution to preserving India's rich artistic and dramatic heritage while introducing timeless works to contemporary cinematic audiences.
Ohh My Dog
: Celebrating the Extraordinary Bond of Unconditional Love and Loyalty
Moving from the complexities of human relationships to the extraordinary purity of the human-animal bond, acclaimed filmmaker Amit Rai presented his Hindi feature ‘
Ohh My Dog’
, a heartwarming yet emotionally charged narrative celebrating empathy, courage, resilience and unconditional affection.
Amit Rai, known for acclaimed films such as
Road to Sangam
,
I-pad
and
OMG 2
, brings together two parallel journeys across India. In Assam, 14-year-old Apu embarks on a desperate quest to rescue his kidnapped dog, Momo, while in Bihar, Oscar, a fiercely loyal dog, sets out to find his kidnapped 15-year-old owner, Prince. Separated by distance but united by an unbreakable bond, their journeys unfold into a heartwarming tale of courage, resilience and unconditional love, celebrating the extraordinary power of devotion to transcend all boundaries.
Sharing the inspiration behind the film's dual narrative, Director Amit Rai spoke about the remarkable emotional honesty of animals and their ability to transcend the prejudices and conditions that often complicate human relationships. "Animals do not carry the burden of prejudice or conditional affection; their loyalty is absolute. Through these parallel journeys, I wanted audiences to experience how empathy and devotion can bridge any distance and overcome every fear," he said.
The Press Conference was moderated by Shri Mahesh Kumar.

title: “Feeling” Before Story: Aquí and The Huntress Carry Human Emotions Across Borders at IFFI 2026
subtitle: Directors Tiago Guedes and Suzanne Andrews Correa discuss films that explore human relationships, emotions and the pursuit of justice
content:
Goa, 23 November 2026
Two very different films at the 57th International Film Festival of India (IFFI) in Goa have one thing in common: both aim to make the audience feel before they understand, placing human emotions at the centre of storytelling. Filmmakers Tiago Guedes and Suzanne Andrews Correa addressed the press during the festival today, sharing insights into their respective films,
Aquí
and
The Huntress (La Cazadora)
.
Aquí
, directed by Tiago Guedes, is a dystopian drama adapted from J. M. Coetzee’s Jesus trilogy, screening in the International Competition section.
The Huntress (La Cazadora
), the debut feature of Mexican-American filmmaker Suzanne Andrews Correa, is a Spanish-language drama thriller inspired by real-life violence against women in Ciudad Juárez, Mexico.
Aquí: A Family Built on Choice
Aquí
, a 2026 film that premiered at the Cannes Film Festival on 18
th
May 2026, is being screened in the International Competition at IFFI 2026, being held from November 20
th
to 28
th
in Goa. Adapted into a single film from Coetzee’s Jesus trilogy, it is set in a society where people begin their lives with no memory of the past, memories are erased and conformity is enforced.
The story follows Simón, who takes in a young boy named David, whom he meets on the journey to this new world. Believing the boy needs a mother, Simón seeks out Inés, who agrees, and the three slowly form an unconventional family. But a society that expects everyone to follow its rules cannot easily accept David, who refuses to fit in. Through his imagination and his desire for freedom, he challenges the world around him. Simón and Inés realise that raising a child is an uncertain journey, full of questions and without easy answers.
Director Tiago Guedes said the film seeks to explore what it means to be human, raising philosophical questions that he believes everyone should reflect upon. On adapting Coetzee’s books, he explained that while reading them, he focussed more on the feelings the story evoked than on the plot itself. This, he said, helps the intensity of the book’s essence reach the screen as a visual experience.
Guedes also explores the idea that family is not always defined by blood relations, but by choices made through a deeply human experience, without turning to religion or gods. The title, which means ‘Here’ in Spanish and Portuguese, reflects this too. As the characters make their choices, the camera subtly shifts from wider to tighter shots, drawing the audience closer to understanding them. Guedes also leaves silences and some ambiguity in the film, so that viewers can form their own interpretations of the story. Aquí is scheduled to be screened in Portugal, Spain and France in January.
The Huntress
: A Cry for Justice
The Huntress (La Cazadora)
is a 2026 Spanish-language drama thriller written and directed by Suzanne Andrews Correa. Adriana Paz stars as a factory worker and assault survivor in Ciudad Juárez, who turns to vigilante justice. The film draws upon the real-life incidents of violence against women and the 2013 case of “Diana, Hunter of the Bus Drivers”, an unidentified vigilante who fatally shot bus drivers amid widespread impunity.
Set in the border region between Mexico and Texas, the film portrays the experiences of women working in factories who faced sexual violence and exploitation. The story unfolds over 24 hours, focusing on the protagonist's experiences and her pursuit of justice.
Correa said her objective was to give viewers a sensory experience of the protagonist’s powerlessness and desperation, so that they can empathise with why she took justice and revenge into her own hands when calls for help went unanswered. The film is also a call for change towards justice and against the crimes against women that continue to prevail.
Correa said the film took her ten years to make, alongside other projects. The journey showed her that filmmaking combines persistence and dedication with the vision to “stay with the story”, and with finding ways to communicate well with the crew, the actors and the audience. Like Guedes, she said her intention was to communicate “feeling” to the audience, rather than focus solely on the story. Although she had initially worried that the story might not appeal to international audiences without the real-life context, but she was both saddened and humbled to see the protagonist’s fear and emotions resonate with audiences across cultures and borders.
The session was moderated by Ms. Sriyanka Chatterjee.
Stories Without Borders
Though one is set in an imagined world without memory and the other in a very real border city,
Aquí
and
The Huntress
meet at the same place: they speak to the heart before the mind. Both directors chose to place feeling ahead of plot, and both use that feeling to ask difficult questions, about human relationships, the meaning of family, personal freedom and the pursuit of justice. Their films illustrate how stories rooted in specific cultural and social contexts can connect with audiences across languages and borders, reflecting the spirit of this year's IFFI theme, ‘Stories Without Borders’.

title: Reimagining the Superhero: Ayan Mukerji and Basil Joseph Converse on Crafting Culturally Rooted Worlds
content:
Goa, 23 November 2026
The extraordinary possibilities of mythology, superheroes and fantastical worlds, rooted in India's rich cultural heritage, took centre stage at an engaging In-conversation session titled ‘The Epic Genres – Mythologies, Superheroes & New Worlds’ at the 57th International Film Festival of India (IFFI) in Goa. Filmmakers Ayan Mukerji and Basil Joseph, in a conversation moderated by Puja Talwar, explored the creative challenges of bringing superheroes and mythological narratives to the screen, the influence of Indian folklore and spirituality, and the evolving role of technology in cinematic storytelling.
Speaking about the challenges of making superhero films in India, Basil Joseph observed that Indian cinema has traditionally portrayed its leading men as larger-than-life figures, often possessing qualities associated with superheroes. This makes creating a distinct superhero cinematic universe particularly challenging. Reflecting on his film
Minnal Murali
, he explained how creative challenges, and budgetary constraints too, can inspire inventive storytelling. Scenes featuring a superhero running with a lungi covering his face and wearing chappals in the movie
Minnal Murali
emerged from such considerations.
Ayan Mukerji shared that the idea of extraordinary powers residing within ordinary people was what initially attracted him to the superhero genre. Discussing the challenge of creating an Indian identity for films that draw inspiration from Western fantasy, he acknowledged that
Brahmastra
initially carried certain Western influences, partly because of his admiration for stories such as Harry Potter. However, incorporating elements of spirituality into the writing helped give the film its distinct Indian identity.
Emphasising the importance of authenticity in filmmaking, Basil Joseph said that filmmakers must remain true to their characters and themselves rather than attempting to make their films appear artificial. He stressed that simplicity and creative honesty are essential, adding that one should never compromise one's own identity in the pursuit of making a film look ‘cool’.
Recalling the making of
Brahmastra
, Ayan Mukerji described the film as a logistically challenging undertaking. He noted that working within restrictions often pushes filmmakers to think beyond conventional approaches and discover more imaginative solutions. Creative challenges, he observed, can become catalysts for innovation rather than obstacles.
The conversation also explored India's deep-rooted relationship with mythology and folklore. Basil Joseph observed that Indian audiences have grown up listening to stories of divine beings and extraordinary powers. Unlike the West, where mythological superheroes are relatively less pervasive in popular storytelling, India has a vast tradition of divine figures who appear to protect and rescue people in times of distress. With an immense reservoir of mythological and folkloric references, filmmakers naturally draw upon stories and experiences absorbed during childhood while creating cinematic worlds.
Ayan Mukerji highlighted how technological advancements have expanded the possibilities of visual storytelling, enabling filmmakers to bring ambitious narratives and fantastical worlds to life. He noted that mythology has always been a constant presence in Indian storytelling, with technology now providing new avenues to present these age-old narratives to contemporary audiences.
Sharing his perspective on the future of filmmaking in the age of Artificial Intelligence, Basil Joseph observed that AI primarily reproduces existing content rather than creating something truly original. He underlined that originality would become increasingly valuable in an era where technology can replicate creative material with ease.
The speakers also discussed how the growth of OTT platforms has transformed the reach of Indian cinema. Basil Joseph pointed out that films made in one language are now finding appreciation across different regions of the country, with audiences able to experience them in their own languages. This growing accessibility, he noted, has opened new avenues for regional cinema to connect with audiences beyond linguistic boundaries.
The conversation offered valuable insights into the evolving landscape of Indian films in the genre, highlighting how technological possibilities, creative ingenuity and an enduring connection with indigenous mythology can come together to create cinematic worlds that are both imaginative and distinctly Indian.

Set in Vachathi, Tamil Nadu, the film unfolds when a power outage leads to the discovery of a sparrow's nest containing eggs inside a village transformer. Despite these challenges, Kathir and the villagers make considerable sacrifices to ensure the nest remains safe.
Through the film, director Joyal Vijay sought to convey that the earth does not belong to human beings alone but is also home to countless other living creatures. Actor V. Jayaprakash shared how being part of the film influenced his personal habits. He said he agreed to the project within minutes of hearing its synopsis, particularly drawn by the fact that it was based on a real-life incident. Reflecting on the film's environmental message, he said his biggest personal takeaway was becoming more conscious of his use of tissue paper, recognising the connection between everyday consumption and the cutting down of trees. He added that the film had encouraged him to minimise its use in his daily life, highlighting how its message had influenced his personal habits.
Producer Rajesh Menon highlighted the emotional appeal of the story and the screenplay's engaging approach to communicating its environmental message. He noted that the film addresses the practical questions and challenges that arise from the villagers' decision to remain without electricity for 35 days, using meaningful dialogues and relatable situations rather than presenting the subject in an overly serious manner. title: Goa’s Future in Cinema: Filmmakers Explore Goa’s Cinematic Potential and its Unique Natural and Cultural Heritage at IFFI 2026
content:
Goa, 23 November 2026
Goa’s potential as a filmmaking destination, the scope for strengthening film-related infrastructure and the importance of preserving its distinctive natural and cultural heritage formed the key themes at an engaging panel discussion titled ‘Goa in Cinema’ at the 57th International Film Festival of India (IFFI).
Bringing together perspectives from Konkani, Hindi and international cinema, the session featured noted Konkani filmmaker Rajendra Talak, Hindi film director and screenwriter Vijay Krishna Acharya, and French actress Marianne Borgo. Film critic Sachin Chatte moderated the discussion
.
Speaking about Goa’s potential to emerge as a prominent filmmaking destination, Vijay Krishna Acharya highlighted the distinctive visual and cultural appeal of the state, which has attracted filmmakers over the years. He observed that Goa possesses a unique and exotic identity that sets it apart from mainstream cinematic locations. Citing the film Kabhi Haan Kabhi Naa, he said that its characters and setting were so organically connected that the story could flourish only in Goa.
Emphasising the need to make filmmaking economically viable, Acharya called for the establishment of a film city that would enable filmmakers to shoot in Goa across different budget categories. “Cost is a crucial consideration in filmmaking. Goa could attract more productions if it offered suitable infrastructure at competitive costs,” he pointed out.  He also highlighted the potential of film schools and film literacy centres in providing local people with access to professional training and employment opportunities in the film industry. Such initiatives, he said, could create a generational impact and help Goa emerge as a unique artistic centre.
Offering a contrasting perspective, Rajendra Talak expressed reservations about the viability of a film city in the state. He observed that the state offered considerable scope for film productions, with its natural landscapes, traditional houses and heritage sites providing a wide range of settings. He also emphasised the importance of ensuring that initiatives to promote filmmaking remain aligned with the preservation of Goa’s cultural identity and natural environment.
Talak pointed out that a large part of Goa remained unexplored as a filming destination. "Hardly ten per cent of Goa has been explored," he said, highlighting the opportunities available for filmmakers to discover new locations and develop stories rooted in the state's diverse settings. He encouraged filmmakers to explore its existing landscapes and find stories that fit naturally into them
.
Marianne Borgo brought the perspective of someone who has made Goa her home. While acknowledging the importance of infrastructure, she underlined the value of the state's natural environment, traditional houses and cultural heritage. She urged filmmakers to approach shooting activities with sensitivity and responsibility, to ensure that Goa's distinctive character is preserved. She also recalled discovering the remarkable talent of Konkani cinema through the film O Mariya, which she watched at IFFI.
The panel also discussed the stereotypical portrayal of Goa and its people in cinema, and underscored the opportunities for filmmakers to explore a wider range of narratives and present a more diverse cinematic representation of Goa.

title: Nirmanjali Unearths Maciej Nowicki's Lesser-Known Contribution to Chandigarh at IFFI 2026
subtitle: Documentary traces the Polish-American architect’s pioneering role in post-Independence Indian urban planning
content:
Goa, 23 November 2026
At a press conference organised by the Press Information Bureau (PIB) at the 57th International Film Festival of India (IFFI) in Goa today, National Award-winning filmmaker Suraj Kumar brought the lesser-known legacy of architect Maciej Nowicki to light through his non-feature documentary,
Nirmanjali: The Chandigarh of Maciej Nowicki
. The film explores Nowicki’s contribution to Chandigarh’s architectural vision, reflected in the city’s distinctive jaali facades, neighbourhood markets and urban landscape.
Rather than imposing rigid monumental structures, Nowicki’s designs responded to India’s climate and community life. He envisioned an artificial water reservoir that later became Sukhna Lake and self-contained residential ‘superblocks’ with schools, parks, markets and community spaces. In 1950, however, just as he was preparing to return to India to implement his vision, Nowicki died in a plane crash. His ideas survived through his drawings, which Swiss architect Pierre Jeanneret recognised and incorporated into the development of Sectors 7 and 8 of Chandigarh.
Reconstructing this lesser-known history required extensive archival research beyond India. With only 20 to 25 of Nowicki’s works preserved at the Chandigarh Architecture Museum, Suraj Kumar traced archival material through vintage editions of
The Tribune
and digitised design notes at North Carolina State University, where Nowicki had headed the Department of Architecture. The research was supported by the Embassy of Poland and the Polish Institute, following a suggestion from the Ambassador of Poland.
Speaking to journalists, Kumar said Nowicki’s 75-year-old blueprints offered valuable lessons for contemporary Indian cities grappling with heat stress and urban sprawl. He emphasised that modern architecture must respond to local climate and human needs.
Produced by Johnsons Suraj Films International (JSFI), led by Suraj Kumar and Dr Garima Singh,
Nirmanjali
features a screenplay by Murtaza Ali Khan, cinematography by Rakesh Rana, editing by Amit Roy, and music by Subhendra Rao and Saskia Rao-de Haas. Veteran actor Victor Banerjee also appears in the film. An alumnus of the Indian Institute of Mass Communication (IIMC), Suraj has 27 years of experience in documentary and feature filmmaking. His previous work includes over 500 documentaries and films such as
Thinking of Him
and
Piplantri
.

title: IICT and Wacom India Sign Strategic MoU at 57th IFFI to Strengthen India-Japan Creative Collaboration
subtitle: Initiative to support AVGC-XR talent through scholarships, professional tools, global mentorship and industry exposure
content:
Goa, 23 November 2026
The Indian Institute of Creative Technologies (IICT), India’s National Centre of Excellence for Animation, Visual Effects, Gaming, Comics and Extended Reality (AVGC-XR), signed an MoU with Wacom India at the 57th International Film Festival of India (IFFI) 2026 to strengthen India-Japan cooperation in creative technologies and skill development.
The partnership aims to expand access to professional tools and industry-led training for Indian students. Under the agreement, 18 students across IICT’s three two-year diploma programmes in Animation Film Design, Interactive Video Game Design & Development, and Post Production & VFX will receive 50% tuition scholarships, along with accommodation assistance for eligible outstation students.
The collaboration will also provide structured mentorship and global exposure through 10 Wacom-branded creative contests and quarterly masterclasses on Manga, Anime and other creative disciplines, led by Japanese and Indian artists and experts, by December 2027. The two institutions will jointly develop a global student portfolio showcase covering digital illustration, concept art, character design, animation and game art, enabling students to build industry-ready portfolios. The agreement also provides for IICT’s integration into Wacom tablet packaging and its Pixel Perch creator platform, subject to mutually agreed implementation plans.
Speaking on the occasion, Dr. Ashish Kulkarni, Founding Director, IICT, said that connecting young creators with global ecosystems is essential to growing India’s creative economy. He noted that the partnership brings together Japan’s strengths in animation, manga and gaming with India’s diverse storytelling heritage, enabling students to create original intellectual property for global audiences.
Dr. Vishwas Deoskar, Chief Executive Officer, IICT, highlighted the importance of practical experience in enhancing employability in the AVGC-XR sector. He said that contests, masterclasses, professional tools and portfolio development would help students work on real-world briefs and demonstrate their industry readiness.
Koji Yano, Global Head of the Creative Experience Unit, Wacom, highlighted the potential for creative collaboration and knowledge exchange between India and Japan across animation, manga, gaming and digital content. He said Wacom’s technologies, including digital ink, would enable young Indian creators to collaborate and participate in global creative partnerships.
About IICT:
The Indian Institute of Creative Technologies (IICT), India’s National Centre of Excellence for Animation, Visual Effects, Gaming, Comics and Extended Reality (AVGC-XR), was established in collaboration with the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting, Government of India, Government of Maharashtra, FICCI and CII. Its first campus began operations at the NFDC Complex in Mumbai, in July 2025, while a permanent campus is being developed at Film City. IICT currently offers 18 courses and has partnered with leading global technology and media companies.

title: From a Mother's Longing to a Child's Fight for Life: Rahma and The Farm Bring Moving Stories to IFFI
subtitle: The Human Urge to Control Comes at a Cost to Other Living Beings: Elif Eda
content:
Goa, 23 November 2026
Stories of motherhood, compassion, human vulnerability and the sanctity of life came into focus at a press conference featuring filmmakers associated with two films showcased under the International Cinema Section of the 57th International Film Festival of India (IFFI), being held in Goa. The films, Rahma and The Farm, explore distinct yet deeply interconnected themes, inviting audiences to look beyond their own struggles and recognise the pain and aspirations of others.
The press conference was attended by Faysal Soysal, director and writer of Rahma; Elif Eda, director and writer of The Farm; and Emre Pekçakır, director of photography of The Farm. The filmmakers shared insights into the creative vision, thematic concerns and experiences behind bringing these compelling stories to the screen.
Rahma: A poignant exploration of motherhood, longing and human connection
Directed and written by Faysal Soysal
, Rahma
follows Meryem, an archaeologist whose longing to become a mother remains unfulfilled despite multiple surgeries and unsuccessful IVF treatments. As hope begins to fade, she considers surrogacy in Georgia, despite her husband İbrahim's reservations. Her life takes an unexpected turn when she encounters Rahma, a nine-year-old Syrian orphan struggling to survive on her own. As Meryem gradually discovers Rahma's situation, an extraordinary bond begins to develop between them, bringing solace and emotional healing into her life.
Speaking about the inspiration behind the film, Faysal Soysal said that the story emerged from a reflection on the intense struggles couples undergo in their desire to have children, juxtaposed with the many children who grow up without families. Through Rahma, he sought to explore the emotional complexities of parenthood, the meaning of family and the unexpected ways in which human relationships can fulfil deep-seated emotional needs.
The Farm: A young girl's courageous stand for the sanctity of life
Written and directed by Elif Eda
,
The Farm
tells the story of 12-year-old İrem, who moves in with her estranged grandmother on a dairy farm following the sudden loss of her parents. Disturbed by the practice of separating newborn calves from their mothers to increase milk production, İrem is unable to reconcile with the cruelty she witnesses. With the help of Halid, an orphan working as an apprentice to the farm's veterinarian, she sets out on a determined mission to free the pregnant cows.
Elif Eda spoke about the central philosophy of the film, emphasising the importance of respecting all forms of life and developing empathy for the suffering of others. She observed that the real danger lies not merely in experiencing pain, but in becoming indifferent to the pain endured by others. Highlighting the sanctity of life on Earth, she reflected on how humans desire to control everything often becomes a source of suffering for other living beings.
The filmmaker explained that she wanted to give a voice to the often-unseen suffering of animals through the film. She also spoke about the challenges of establishing oneself as a woman director in the film industry, highlighting the additional difficulties women encounter while pursuing their creative aspirations.
Sharing his experience of working on The Farm, Director of Photography Emre Pekçakır spoke about the unique challenges he faced while filming the cows. Recalling the production experience, he said that he spent considerable time on the farms, staying close to the animals to capture their behaviour and the nuances of their surroundings. Despite the challenges, he described the experience of shooting with the animals as an enjoyable and enriching part of the filmmaking process.
Together,
Rahman
and
The Farm
offer moving reflections on compassion, belonging and empathy, reminding audiences to look beyond their own circumstances and acknowledge the lives and struggles of others.

title: NHAI’s Barrier-less MLFF Tolling System Boosts Net Toll Revenue by 19.84% Across Operational Fee Plazas
subtitle: Cumulative performance across seven MLFF plazas indicates an increase of 19.84% in net revenue, compared to the corresponding pre-MLFF baseline. Transaction volumes also registered significant growth

content:
Transforming Electronic Toll Collection system in the country, the implementation of Barrier-Less Tolling through Multi-Lane Free Flow (MLFF) technology is delivering significant benefits to the National Highway commuters as well as the Government, with a substantial increase in net toll revenue and transaction volumes across operational plazas. The barrier-less initiative has demonstrated the potential of technology-driven tolling to transform National Highway travel by eliminating the need for vehicles to stop at toll plazas. The system facilitates seamless movement of vehicles, reduces congestion and travel time, minimises fuel consumption and vehicular emissions, and enhances transparency and efficiency in toll collection.
Following the successful launch on 1st May 2026 at Choryasi Fee Plaza in Gujarat, the MLFF system has progressively been operationalised at eight more fee plazas, namely Mundka, Daulatpura, Gharaunda, Manoharpura, Shahjahanpur, Paranur, Nemili and Chenasamudram. As on 31 October 2026, the cumulative performance across these seven plazas (excluding Nemili and Chenasamudram which went live in November 2026) indicates an increase of 19.84% in net revenue to NHAI, compared to the corresponding pre-MLFF baseline. Transaction volumes have also registered significant growth.

In absolute terms, the seven plazas have generated cumulative net revenue of around ₹538.95 crore, as against the corresponding pre-MLFF benchmark of approximately ₹449.72 crore, representing additional net revenue of about ₹89.23 crore.
The increase in revenue is particularly noteworthy as it has been achieved alongside a substantial increase in transaction volumes and reduction in collection cost. This demonstrates that MLFF is not merely facilitating faster toll collection but is also improving the efficiency and coverage of toll collection, thereby reducing revenue leakage and ensuring better realisation of the applicable user fee.
Further, around 60% of the value of e-notices issued across these plazas has already been realised. This reflects the effectiveness of technology-enabled enforcement in ensuring compliance and recovering user fees even from vehicles that initially evade payment.
Enforcement against toll evasion
While the transition to barrier-less tolling has resulted in significant operational and financial gains, instances have also been reported of certain vehicle owners deliberately masking, concealing or tampering with their vehicle registration number plates to evade toll payment. NHAI has taken serious cognizance of such instances and is closely coordinating with the concerned State Governments and enforcement agencies to ensure strict action against such defaulters. Police Check Posts have been established at certain MLFF locations, including Gharaunda Fee Plaza, where vehicles found indulging in such practices are being intercepted and challaned under the relevant provisions of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988.
Simultaneously, NHAI is deploying AI-based technological solutions, including Vehicle Fingerprinting and integration with the VAHAN database, to identify such vehicles and trace their registered owners. E-notices are being issued for recovery of unpaid user fees and applicable VAHAN services are being restricted in cases where such notices remain unpaid, in accordance with the prescribed enforcement framework.
NHAI remains committed to expanding barrier-less tolling across the National Highway network to provide greater convenience, faster and seamless journeys and an improved travel experience to National Highway users. At the same time, the Authority will continue to strengthen technology-driven monitoring and enforcement in coordination with State Governments to prevent toll evasion, safeguard public revenue and ensure compliance by all highway users.

title: Joint workshop of the Ministries of Agriculture and Rural Development, on their role in eradication of poverty, concludes in Delhi under the chairmanship of Union Minister Shri Shivraj Singh Chouhan
subtitle:
Encouraging officers and employees, Union Minister Shri Shivraj Singh Chouhan says: “You have not merely framed schemes; you have built the nation. You are the true drivers of this development journey”

“Extreme poverty has declined from 27.1% to 2.6%; our resolve is to lift those still left behind out of poverty”: Shri Shivraj Singh Chouhan

“Agriculture growth rate reaches a historic 4.45%, taking India’s farm sector beyond even the Green Revolution era”: Union Minister Shri Shivraj Singh Chouhan

“Lakhpati Didis, permanent houses, rural roads, Viksit Bharat - G RAM G and watershed development have transformed the lives of the rural poor”: Shri Shivraj Singh

date:

content:
Under the visionary leadership of Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi, India has achieved unprecedented, extraordinary and historic milestones in the field of poverty eradication. According to the World Bank’s recent report, nearly 500 million people in the country have moved out of poverty, while the rate of extreme poverty has declined from 27.1 per cent to just 2.6 per cent. This remarkable progress reflects the contribution of several sectors and government initiatives, particularly agriculture and allied activities, agricultural research, land resources and rural development. To assess the role played by these areas in the achievement and discuss the strategy for the road ahead, a special one-day workshop was organised today at the Dr Ambedkar International Centre in New Delhi. The joint workshop was chaired by Union Minister for Agriculture and Farmers’ Welfare, and Rural Development, Shri Shivraj Singh Chouhan. Union Minister of State for Agriculture and Farmers’ Welfare Shri Bhagirath Choudhary and Union Minister of State for Rural Development Shri Kamlesh Paswan also participated. Describing the country’s progress, Shri Chouhan called it an “extraordinary, unimaginable and unprecedented miracle”.
The workshop brought together the senior-most officials of all four departments whose work and initiatives were being reviewed. Those present included Secretary, Department of Agriculture and Farmers’ Welfare, Shri Atish Chandra; Secretary, Department of Rural Development, Shri Rohit Kansal; Secretary, Department of Land Resources, Shri Dilip Kumar; and Secretary, Department of Agricultural Research and Education (DARE) and Director General of the Indian Council of Agricultural Research (ICAR), Dr M. L. Jat. Senior officials and scientists from the four departments also attended, along with Section Officers, Assistant Section Officers and a large number of other officers and employees. The participation of staff across different levels reflected the workshop’s focus not only on reviewing departmental achievements, but also on recognising the contribution of those involved in taking policies and schemes from the planning stage to implementation.
Lifting 500 million people out of poverty, more than the population of the United States, is a miracle
Addressing officers and employees of the Department of Agriculture and Farmers’ Welfare, ICAR, Department of Rural Development and Department of Land Resources, Union Minister Shri Shivraj Singh Chouhan said that the achievement India had secured under the leadership and guidance of Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi was truly extraordinary, remarkable and unimaginable. The World Bank itself had acknowledged that no other country in the world had reduced poverty at such a rapid pace. The fact that nearly 500 million people had moved above the poverty line represented a historic development, particularly given the scale of the population involved. Shri Chouhan said that this progress was the result of the Prime Minister’s leadership, vision and hard work, but it was also important to recognise the contribution made by every officer and employee in the two ministries. The achievement, he stressed, was not the work of any one individual or department; it reflected the collective effort of people working across the government machinery to deliver development and improve lives.
“You have not merely framed schemes; you have built the nation”: Celebrate this achievement
Encouraging officers and employees, Union Minister Shri Chouhan said that this success had not come about on its own. Behind it lay the hard work, dedication and sustained efforts of everyone who had contributed to the implementation of government programmes. He urged those attending the workshop to participate with a sense of joy and celebration, observing that when the country had achieved something so significant, the happiness and pride it inspired should also be visible on their faces. Shri Chouhan recalled that the Prime Minister had emphasised that “you have not merely framed schemes; you have built the nation”. He explained that review meetings are generally attended by senior officials, but he had consciously decided to make this workshop different. He wanted colleagues at every level, from Section Officers and Assistant Section Officers to Secretaries, to be present because they were the foundation stones of the administrative system and the work on files began at these levels. He told the employees that they were not merely witnesses to the country’s development journey, but its true drivers and participants. Demonstrating his intention to engage directly with them, Shri Chouhan left the stage and sat among the audience, speaking with employees and seeking to understand their experiences on the ground and their suggestions.
Resolve to bring those still left behind out of poverty
Union Minister Shri Shivraj Singh Chouhan said that people work not merely to earn a livelihood, but also to find purpose in their lives and serve the people of the country. He observed that every stage in the journey of a government scheme involves the contribution of employees. Whether a scheme is developed from the grassroots, considered and approved by the Cabinet, or eventually implemented on the ground, the efforts of people working at different levels are essential to its success. He said that two major commitments made by the Prime Minister now lay before the nation. The first was to ensure that those who had already risen above the poverty line did not fall back below it under any circumstances. The second was to rapidly bring the remaining 2.6 to 2.7 per cent of the population out of poverty and improve their standard of living. Shri Chouhan emphasised that the progress achieved so far must be protected, while the government continued working to reach those who had yet to benefit sufficiently from the country’s development. The task ahead, therefore, was both to sustain the gains made and to ensure that the remaining people were also able to lead better lives.
Agriculture growth rate reaches a historic 4.45%; ICAR research delivers returns of 13.85 times the investment
Highlighting the achievements of the agriculture sector, Union Minister Shri Chouhan said that the past 12 years had witnessed remarkable progress, with work being undertaken in agriculture that the country could take pride in. He pointed out that even during the Green Revolution, the agriculture growth rate generally remained in the range of 3 to 3.5 per cent. India’s decadal agriculture growth rate had now reached the historic level of 4.45 per cent, surpassing the levels recorded during that period. Among the key initiatives contributing to the sector’s progress, he highlighted the direct assistance of more than ₹4.66 lakh crore provided through the PM-KISAN Samman Nidhi under the Department of Agriculture and Farmers’ Welfare. The sector had also recorded foodgrain production of 376.56 million tonnes and horticulture production of 386.91 million tonnes. Affordable agricultural credit, crop insurance, natural farming, the establishment of 10,000 Farmer Producer Organisations (FPOs) and digital initiatives such as AgriStack had further supported farmers and contributed to increasing their incomes. Together, these measures reflected the progress made in strengthening agricultural production and improving the support available to farmers.
A presentation by the Department of Agricultural Research and Education (DARE/ICAR) highlighted the economic returns generated by scientific research and innovation. It stated that every rupee invested in agricultural research and education had yielded an economic benefit of ₹13.85, while investment in animal husbandry research had generated a return of ₹20.81. Since 2014, a total of 3,436 new crop varieties had been released, of which 93 per cent were climate-resilient. The presentation also highlighted the contribution of biofortified crop varieties, fish production of 19.78 million tonnes and the availability of more than 500 agricultural machines. In addition, digital outreach through Krishi Vigyan Kendras (KVKs) was reaching five crore farmers every year. These research-led developments, technological interventions and knowledge-sharing efforts had helped strengthen the rural economy and extend the benefits of agricultural science to farmers across the country.
Rural development and DoLR schemes have transformed the lives of villages and the rural poor
The workshop also examined in detail the impact of schemes implemented by the Department of Rural Development and the Department of Land Resources. Shri Chouhan said that these departments had played a highly significant role in the country's progress towards poverty eradication. Presentations highlighted the reach of several rural development initiatives. Under the Deendayal Antyodaya Yojana - National Rural Livelihoods Mission, more than 10 crore women had been connected with self-help groups, and 3.76 crore women had so far become ‘Lakhpati Didis’. The Pradhan Mantri Awaas Yojana - Gramin (PMAY-G) had enabled the construction of 3.99 crore permanent houses, while the Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana (PMGSY) had created a network of 7.99 lakh kilometres of all-weather rural roads. Under Viksit Bharat - G RAM G (VB-G RAM G), rural households are now assured of 125 days of employment. Social assistance programmes and 99.9 per cent transparency in Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT) have also helped empower the last person in the queue. These initiatives have contributed to changing the lives of rural families by supporting livelihoods, providing housing, improving connectivity and strengthening the delivery of assistance to beneficiaries.
Under the Department of Land Resources (DoLR), the watershed development component of the Pradhan Mantri Krishi Sinchayee Yojana (WDC-PMKSY) has supported water conservation and land improvement works across 3.40 crore hectares. These interventions have directly benefited 61.15 lakh farmers. The work has contributed to an increase in irrigated areas and milk production, while farmers’ average annual incomes have recorded growth of up to 70 per cent. The figures presented at the workshop highlighted the contribution of watershed development to improving land and water resources, strengthening agricultural activity and supporting the livelihoods of farming communities. The programme's impact was also reflected in the number of farmers who had directly benefited from these interventions and the reported improvement in their annual incomes.
Suggestions sought to improve budgets and schemes; call to take achievements to the public
During the concluding session of the workshop, Union Minister Shri Shivraj Singh Chouhan extended an open invitation to officers and employees to share their ideas and suggestions. He emphasised that the achievements made so far did not mean there was no scope for further improvement. Several useful suggestions had already been received on schemes such as PM-KISAN and e-NAM. He encouraged everyone to write to him without hesitation if they had any ideas concerning the budget, changes to existing schemes or the introduction of new initiatives that could help increase farmers’ incomes. Shri Chouhan said that he would also hold informal, department-wise meetings with employees working at lower levels in the future. As the head of the department, he assured colleagues that he would remain accessible and approachable to everyone, regardless of their position or level of responsibility. He invited them to contribute their practical experience and ideas to the process of improving government programmes and making them more effective.
Shri Chouhan also placed particular emphasis on the need to ensure that the departments’ achievements and public welfare initiatives did not remain confined to files and formal communications, but were effectively taken to the people and farmers. He said that communicating the work being done by the departments and its impact on people's lives was an important responsibility. Giving an example, he observed that when officials go directly to the ground and engage with people, the positive message reaches the entire country. He stressed that the development journey was far from over and that the targets set for 2029, 2030–31 and ‘Viksit Bharat @2047’ had to be achieved on time. Referring to the Free Trade Agreements (FTAs), he said that the next objective was to enable Indian agricultural products to make their mark in markets across the world. The country now had to build on the progress achieved in agriculture and ensure that its products reached and competed successfully in global markets.
