title: Nayi Chetna 5.0 to be Launched on 25 November
subtitle: Joint Inter-Ministerial Advisory involving 15 Ministries/Departments and Signed Quadripartite MoU on Violence-Free Village Initiative to be Unveiled
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                23 NOV 2026 10:28AM by PIB Delhi
content:
The Ministry of Rural Development will launch the fifth edition of its national gender campaign, Nayi Chetna – Pahal Badlav Ki, on 25 November 2026, marking the International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women. The month-long campaign will be implemented nationwide from 25 November to 23 December 2026 under the Deendayal Antyodaya Yojana–National Rural Livelihoods Mission (DAY-NRLM).
Shri Shivraj Singh Chouhan, Hon’ble Union Minister of Rural Development and Agriculture & Farmers’ Welfare, will inaugurate the national launch in the presence of Smt. Annpurna Devi, Hon’ble Union Minister of Women and Child Development. The event will also witness the presence of Shri Kamlesh Paswan, Hon’ble Minister of State, Rural Development along with senior officials of participating Ministries, representatives of State Governments, development partners and women leaders from community institutions across the country.
The launch will take place at 2:00 PM at Bharat Ratna C. Subramaniam Auditorium, NASC Complex, Dev Prakash Shastri Marg, Pusa, New Delhi – 110012.
The theme of Nayi Chetna 5.0, “From Access to Agency: Empowering Women through Livelihoods and Equal Opportunities for a Viksit Bharat,” highlights the importance of women’s access and mobility as critical enablers of economic empowerment, livelihood participation and independent decision-making.
Four interconnected areas of focus
Nayi Chetna 5.0 will place women’s economic empowerment at the centre of its approach, with a focus on four interconnected areas: recognising women as economic contributors, strengthening women’s access to and control over assets, promoting safe mobility, and redistributing unpaid care work. Particular emphasis will be placed on addressing barriers that restrict women’s access to livelihood opportunities, markets, financial services, public spaces and essential services, and their ability to move freely, safely and independently. The campaign aims to move beyond awareness generation towards coordinated action and measurable improvements in women’s economic participation, agency and decision-making.
The highlights of the event
Joint Inter-Ministerial Advisory involving 15 Ministries/Departments
A key highlight of the national launch will be the release of a Joint Inter-Ministerial Advisory involving 15 Ministries/Departments. The Advisory will reflect a shared commitment to advance the objectives of Nayi Chetna 5.0 through coordinated action and convergence. It will provide a framework for Ministries and Departments to align their schemes, programmes, institutional mechanisms and frontline networks with the campaign’s objectives. It will seek to strengthen coordinated interventions at the national, State, district and community levels, particularly to improve women’s access to livelihoods, assets, financial services, safe mobility, essential services and institutional support.
Signed Quadripartite MoU on Violence-Free Village Initiative
The event will also feature the release of the signed Quadripartite Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) on the Violence-Free Village Initiative, among the Ministry of Rural Development, Ministry of Women and Child Development, Department of Justice and National Legal Services Authority (NALSA). The MoU will provide a framework for coordinated institutional action to prevent and respond to gender-based violence at the community level. It is intended to strengthen convergence between community institutions, legal services authorities and relevant government mechanisms, including awareness of legal rights, access to justice, institutional support and collective action towards building violence-free villages.
Strengthening community institutions and women’s leadership
DAY-NRLM’s extensive network of Self-Help Groups (SHGs), Village Organisations (VOs), Cluster Level Federations (CLFs), Gender Resource Centres (GRCs) and other community institutions will play a central role in the implementation of Nayi Chetna 5.0. During the launch, new Gender Resource Centres will be inaugurated as community-level platforms to facilitate access to services, entitlements, support systems and grievance redressal mechanisms. SHG women leaders from different States will share their experiences, innovations and perspectives on strengthening women’s collective action and leadership.
The programme will also feature two panel discussions during the day. The first panel, “Advancing Ministerial Convergence through Gender Resource Centres (GRCs), One Stop Centres (OSCs), Legal Services Authority (LSA), and Health System,” will bring together representatives from relevant Ministries and institutions to deliberate on strengthening convergence and coordinated responses to women’s concerns. The second panel, “Women Leaders from the Field: Experiences, Innovations and the Way Forward,” will provide a platform for grassroots women leaders to share their experiences and recommendations.
Nayi Chetna 4.0 Assessment Report
The Nayi Chetna 4.0 Assessment Report will be released during the national launch. The report will present the assessment of the previous edition and its key learnings to inform and strengthen future campaign interventions.
The programme will also include the screening of State-level videos and presentations of good practices, highlighting community-led initiatives and approaches towards gender equality. Video resources developed for the campaign will also be launched.
Spearheaded by DAY-NRLM, Ministry of Rural Development, Nayi Chetna has evolved since its inception in 2022 into a nationwide collective movement to address gender-based violence (GBV), challenge discriminatory social norms and advance gender equality. Through Nayi Chetna 5.0, the Ministry seeks to strengthen collective action among Ministries, State Governments, community institutions and other stakeholders to create an enabling environment for women’s economic participation, safety and agency. The campaign will also encourage the active engagement of men, boys and youth in challenging discriminatory social norms and promoting equality and shared responsibility.

title: New advanced material developed by incorporating metallic nanowires into MOFs can harness sunlight to degrade pollutants
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                23 NOV 2026 3:49PM by PIB Delhi
content:
A novel material developed by scientists through
incorporating metallic nanowires into
metal–organic framework (MOF), can harness a broad range of light wavelengths to efficiently degrade environmental pollutants like pyrene, a persistent polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon (PAH).
Pyrene is a persistent pollutant and cause serious environmental problems because it is toxic to organisms and difficult to remediate. Scientists have been exploring ways of remediating Pyrene using Metal organic Frameworks (MOF), molecular constructions with large spaces through which gases and other chemicals can flow, the importance of which was recognized through the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2026.
One-dimensional metallic nanowires are promising materials for capturing and using light because they can conduct electricity efficiently and interact strongly with light. Their unique structure helps them absorb more light. These properties make them attractive for developing advanced light-driven technologies. In particular, plasmonic photocatalysis offers a promising approach for sustainable energy and environmental applications because it can effectively utilize both visible and near-infrared light. Thus, incorporating metallic nanowires into MOFs can synergistically integrate the properties of both components.
Researchers from the Institute of Advanced Study in Science and Technology (IASST), Guwahati, an Autonomous Institute under the Department of Science & Technology (DST), Govt. of India have developed an isoreticular (having the same underlying network topology as) metal–organic framework-8 (IRMOF-8)-confined copper nanowire (Cu NW)-based hybrid material that incorporates palladium (Pd) nanostructures to enhance light absorption and photocatalytic activity.
At the same time, aluminum (Al) was chosen as an alternative to Pd because of its abundance, cost-effectiveness, and energetic plasmonic properties. The porous IRMOF-8 framework provides a confined environment for the nanowires, enabling close interactions among the components and facilitating efficient charge transfer.
The incorporation of Pd significantly enhanced broadband light absorption via plasmonic interactions, while the earth-abundant Al-based system formed a promising antenna-reactor platform, thereby promoting interfacial charge transfer and photocatalytic disintegration of polybenzenoid hydrocarbon pollutants.
The optimized integration of Pd into the copper nanowire (Cu NW) in metal–organic framework-8 (IRMOF-8) achieved 99% and Al into copper nanowire (Cu NW) in metal–organic framework-8 (IRMOF-8) achieved 85% removal of pyrene under the investigated irradiation and ultrasonication conditions.
Fig:
Schematic representation of the photocatalytic materials designed to target the disintegration of pyrene using solar energy combined with ultrasonication frequencies.
The findings of this study led by Prof. Devasish Chowdhury, together with his PhD scholar Ms. Netra Prova Baruah, in collaboration with Prof. Mojibur R. Khan, Ms. Mandira Thakur, Ms. Ipsah Akhtar, Mr. Rahul Sonkar, and Prof. Arundhuti Devi recently published in ACS Applied Energy Materials,
present a notable strategy for designing MOF-confined plasmonic nanomaterials for solar-harvesting photocatalysis and environmental remediation, especially in aquatic ecosystems.
“The research is also an effort to develop aluminum (Al) -based system, which exhibited substantial photocatalytic performance, accentuating its potential to reduce reliance on noble metals,” said Prof. Chowdhury.

title: Scientists discover a rare stellar fossil that preserves clues to the universe's first generations of stars
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                23 NOV 2026 3:46PM by PIB Delhi
content:
Astronomers have discovered a rare ancient star, HE 1153−0518, whose chemical composition preserves the signatures of some of the earliest generations of stars in the Universe.
The earliest generations of stars in the Universe formed only a few hundred million years after the Big Bang. Although those massive stars no longer exist, they enriched the primordial gas with newly synthesized elements before ending their lives in supernovae explosions.
Ancient metal-poor stars that formed from this enriched gas preserve these chemical signatures and therefore act as "stellar fossils," allowing astronomers to reconstruct the history of the early Universe. Hence the discovery of such a rare stellar fossil provides important clues to the nucleosynthesis processes that enriched the primordial Universe and shaped the chemical evolution of our Galaxy.
Using high-resolution spectroscopic data collected at Subaru telescope at Hawaii, together with recent astrometric and photometric data, a team from the Indian Institute of Astrophysics (IIA), Bengaluru, an Autonomous Institute of the Department of Science and Technology (DST) and Dakshin Kamrup College, Assam, determined the atmospheric properties and chemical abundances of the star with high precision. These measurements of atmospheric properties and chemical abundances enable a comprehensive investigation of the nucleosynthetic history of how its various elements were synthesized in nuclear reactions and its evolutionary status.
Fig
: Yoon-Beers diagram showing the absolute carbon abundance, A(C), as a function of metallicity, [Fe/H], for carbon-enhanced metal-poor (CEMP) stars.  The coloured ellipses show the approximate locations of the different groups as indicated. The large yellow star marks HE 1153-0518 from this work.  The solid black line represents the CEMP classification boundary corresponding to [C/Fe] = +0.7.
The study identifies HE 1153−0518 as a previously unknown sub-class of carbon-enhanced metal-poor (CEMP) stars called CEMP-no star. Among the CEMP stars, CEMP-no stars form a sub-group that exhibits enhancement in carbon and is deficient in heavy elements. These stars form a rare class of stellar fossils that provides a direct window into the earliest phases of Galactic evolution. The star HE 1153-0518 contains only about one-thousandth of the Sun's iron abundance, yet is remarkably rich in carbon and sodium while being severely deficient in heavy elements produced by neutron-capture nucleosynthesis.
The study also measures a low carbon isotopic (12C/13C) ratio, indicating that the star has experienced significant internal mixing of its gas. Its spectral energy distribution in the optical and infrared wavebands reveals evidence of excess infrared emission, suggesting the possible presence of circumstellar dust. Together, these observational characteristics provide valuable insights into both the intrinsic evolution of the star and the chemical environment from which it formed.
"Ancient metal-poor stars are among the oldest surviving objects in our Galaxy. They formed from gas that had been enriched by the very first stellar explosions. Their chemical composition allows us to investigate nucleosynthesis that occurred more than 13 billion years ago. Discoveries such as HE 1153−0518 bring us closer to understanding how the first generations of stars enriched the universe with the elements that later became the building blocks of stars, planets and life.” explained Aruna Goswami of the Indian IIA and a co-author of the study.
To understand the origin of the observed abundance pattern, the authors compare the measured elemental abundances with predictions from theoretical nucleosynthesis models. Partha Pratim Goswami, from Dakshin Kamrup College and the lead author of the study, explains the broader significance of the discovery: "Every newly discovered chemically primitive star helps us reconstruct the earliest history of the Milky Way and the lives of the first stars. These stellar fossils provide some of the strongest observational constraints on models of stellar nucleosynthesis and Galactic chemical evolution."
This discovery published in journal the Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society (MNRAS), expands the growing inventory of stellar fossils that preserve the chemical record of the early Universe. The study demonstrates how high-resolution stellar spectroscopy continues to uncover relics of the early Milky Way, a field of study that has long been pursued at the Indian Institute of Astrophysics, an autonomous institution under the Department of Science and Technology, Government of India. By decoding the elemental compositions of ancient stars, astronomers can investigate events that occurred more than 13 billion years ago, well before the formation of the Sun and the Solar System.

title: From Manual Sewer Cleaning to Robotic Sanitation Operations
subtitle: NAMASTE Training Supports a Safer and More Dignified Occupational Transition
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                23 NOV 2026 6:09PM by PIB Delhi
content:
Transitioning sanitation workers from hazardous manual cleaning to mechanised sanitation operations is an important step towards improving occupational safety, health and dignity. Training and access to technology can help workers build technical skills and undertake sanitation work in safer conditions.
Raja (Name Changed), a 41-year-old Scheduled Caste sanitation worker from Mysuru, Karnataka, spent nearly 15 years engaged in manual sewer and septic tank cleaning, with prolonged direct exposure to hazardous waste. Inadequate access to machinery and training, along with the health challenges associated with toxic exposure, affected his physical well-being. With limited education and his family dependent on his income, opportunities to move to safer work remained constrained.
With an interest in mechanised sanitation operations, he received Occupational Safety and Mechanised Sanitation Training under the National Action for Mechanised Sanitation Ecosystem (NAMASTE) Scheme in 2026, as part of a batch of 45 sanitation workers. The training covered occupational health hazards, safe work practices and operation of the Bandicoot robotic sanitation system.
Following the training, Rajagopala is now working as a Bandicoot robotic sanitation system operator, marking a significant shift from manual sewer cleaning to machine-based sanitation operations. His new role enables him to undertake sanitation work with reduced direct exposure to hazardous waste and in a safer, more dignified environment.
His journey highlights how occupational safety training and mechanised equipment under the NAMASTE Scheme can support sanitation workers in acquiring technical skills, improving work conditions and moving towards safer and dignified livelihoods.

More than 130 stalls across seven thematic zones — कला आँगन, प्रकाश चौक, पूजा पथ, सजावट बाज़ार, घराना, स्वाद चौक and मंच — offered visitors a vibrant experience of traditional crafts, textiles, home décor, festive products, indigenous creations and regional culinary traditions.
A Senior Official in the Ministry said the Mela provided a dedicated platform to artisans and beneficiaries belonging to Scheduled Castes, Other Backward Classes, Safai Karamcharis and persons with disabilities to showcase their products, engage directly with consumers and expand their market opportunities.
The participating artisans were supported through the Ministry's apex corporations, namely National Scheduled Castes Finance and Development Corporation (NSFDC), National Backward Classes Finance and Development Corporation (NBCFDC), National Safai Karamcharis Finance and Development Corporation (NSKFDC) and National Divyangjan Finance and Development Corporation (NDFDC), the Official said.
The Mela was inaugurated by Hon’ble Union Minister for Social Justice and Empowerment, Dr. Virendra Kumar, on November 2, 2026. During his visit, the Minister toured the stalls, interacted with artisans and appreciated their craftsmanship, creativity and entrepreneurial spirit, the Official said.
Dr Kumar highlighted the significance of providing platforms that enable artisans to showcase their products, strengthen livelihood opportunities and contribute towards an inclusive and self-reliant India, he further said.
The Official said the Mela also marked the first-ever joint Shilp Utsav initiative of the Department of Social Justice and Empowerment (DoSJE) and the Department of Empowerment of Persons with Disabilities (DEPwD), bringing traditional artisans and creative talent of persons with disabilities together on an inclusive platform through Bharat TULIP and Purple Fest.
Union Minister of State for Social Justice and Empowerment, Shri Ramdas Athawale, visited the Mela on November 6, 2026, and visited the stalls showcasing handicrafts, handloom products, traditional textiles, festive decorations, lamps, home décor and other indigenous products, the Official said.
The Minister interacted with participating artisans and appreciated the initiative for creating market linkages and strengthening livelihood opportunities, he said. He emphasised the Government's commitment towards inclusive socio-economic development and empowering communities through entrepreneurship and self-employment, the Official added.
Smt. Nimuben Jayantibhai Bambhaniya, Union Minister of State for Consumer Affairs, Food and Public Distribution, also visited Mela along with the Union MoS Shri Athawale.
Secretary, Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment, Shri Sudhansh Pant, visited the Mela on November 5, 2026, and interacted with participating artisans and entrepreneurs. He inspected the stalls and appreciated the diversity and quality of products being showcased.
The Secretary underscored the importance of Shilp Samagam in connecting traditional artisans with consumers, facilitating market access and promoting sustainable livelihood opportunities. He encouraged citizens and visitors to support the artisans by appreciating and purchasing their products, the Official said.
The Mela also witnessed visits by senior officials and dignitaries, who engaged with artisans and reviewed the range of products and activities being showcased, the Official said.
The Official said the visits reaffirmed the Ministry's commitment towards promoting entrepreneurship, strengthening market access and creating opportunities for beneficiaries to achieve economic empowerment through their skills and traditional knowledge.
The Official said a major attraction throughout the 15 days was the series of cultural programmes held every evening at the मंच. Artists and performing groups from different States presented folk dances, traditional music and regional art forms, offering visitors a glimpse into India's diverse cultural traditions.
The cultural evenings added to the festive atmosphere of the Mela and fostered cultural exchange and appreciation of India's pluralistic heritage, the Official said.
The Official said the Mela also provided opportunities for artisans to explore wider market reach through initiatives such as Bharat TULIP, which connects artisans with e-commerce platforms, and Purple Fest, which celebrates the creativity and capabilities of persons with disabilities and promotes inclusion and equal opportunities.
It is pertinent to mention that since 2022, the Ministry has been organising Shilp Samagam Melas, benefiting more than 1,000 artisans from Scheduled Castes, Other Backward Classes and Safai Karamchari communities through opportunities to exhibit and market their products.
The initiative continues to support entrepreneurship, self-employment, livelihood generation and the socio-economic empowerment of beneficiary communities, he said.
Expressing satisfaction, the Official said the successful conclusion of Shilp Samagam Mela 2026, with sales of ₹1,13,34,681 over 15 days, underscores the growing public appreciation for traditional craftsmanship and the importance of sustained platforms that connect artisans directly with consumers.
The Mela reflects the Ministry's continued efforts towards promoting inclusive growth, preserving India's cultural heritage and advancing economic empowerment through entrepreneurship and market-driven opportunities, he concluded.

Access to financial assistance in higher education can help scholars pursue advanced research, develop academic skills and work towards long-term professional aspirations, particularly when financial constraints otherwise limit their opportunities.

The fellowship has brought positive changes in his educational, financial and personal life, helping him make progress towards completing his doctoral research and pursuing his future career aspirations.

title: Data Users Conference on the New Series of Gross Domestic Product (GDP), Consumer Price Index (CPI) and Index of Industrial Production (IIP) Held in Mumbai on 23 November 2026
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                23 NOV 2026 5:32PM by PIB Delhi
content:
The The Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI), with the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) as the Knowledge Partner, organised a “Data Users Conference on the New Series of Gross Domestic Product (GDP), Consumer Price Index (CPI) and Index of Industrial Production (IIP)” on 23 November 2026 at Mumbai. Following the release of revised series of GDP, CPI and IIP at different points during 2026, the conference was organised to familiarise data users with the methodological changes, data sources and key improvements incorporated in each of the revised series. It also aimed to facilitate a better understanding of these changes and their implications for the resulting estimates.
The conference brought together representatives of the Reserve Bank of India (RBI), SEBI, economists, forecasters, credit rating agencies, experts from financial institutions and the banking sector, academia, research institutions, industry and investor organisations, users of official statistics and senior officials of the Central and State Governments. The inaugural session comprised welcome remarks by Dr. Dalip Singh, Director General (Central Statistics), MoSPI; the setting of the context by Dr. Saurabh Garg, Secretary, MoSPI; the inaugural address by Dr. Poonam Gupta, Deputy Governor, RBI; the keynote address by Shri Deepak Parekh, Former Chairman, HDFC; and the vote of thanks by Shri Siddhartha Kundu, ADG, National Accounts Division, MoSPI. A booklet containing brief concept notes on the revised series of these indices was shared with the participants.
Dr. Dalip Singh,
Director General (Central Statistics), in his welcome address, noted that macroeconomic statistics form the foundation of economic analysis, policy making and informed decision making and that GDP, CPI and IIP together provide a comprehensive measure of economic activity and growth. He observed that, as the structure of the economy, production processes, consumption patterns and technology continue to evolve, the statistical system must evolve continuously to remain representative of prevailing economic realities. He recalled that MoSPI had completed the base revision of these three indicators and launched the new series during 2026, with greater use of administrative and survey-based data, wider coverage and important methodological improvements and acknowledged the contribution of expert committees, central ministries, State Governments, RBI and other institutions.
Dr. Saurabh Garg,
Secretary, MoSPI, while setting the context, noted that the conference was being held in Mumbai after about a year, this time after the completion of the base revision exercise, with the first-quarter GDP estimates of the new series already released and the second-quarter estimates due shortly. He stated that the two-year exercise had been made possible by the support of several expert committees, other ministries and departments, State Governments, the RBI and other regulatory agencies. Looking ahead, he outlined the Ministry’s priorities, including the rebasing of Gross State Domestic Product to 2022-23 and the development of District Domestic Product estimates for more granular decision making; preparation for the implementation of the System of National Accounts (SNA) 2025, with its focus on well-being and distributional accounts, recognition  of data as an asset and valuation of natural resources; the development of satellite accounts for the space, culture, digital and city economies; the stabilisation of the Index of Services Production; and the updating of national industrial and product classifications, in support of timely, relevant and evidence-based policy making towards the goal of Viksit Bharat 2047.
Dr. Poonam Gupta,
Deputy Governor, RBI, in her inaugural address, congratulated MoSPI on completing the base revision of the three series in a timely manner and commended the Ministry’s extensive consultations with users. She observed that a base revision is not merely a routine technical update but records important shifts in the structure of the economy, consumption behaviour and the sources of growth, the better measurement of which is important for policy making. She highlighted the key features of the revised series — the use of double deflation and a wider range of administrative data in the national accounts, the alignment of demand- and supply-side GDP estimates through the Supply-Use Table framework, the updated weighting pattern and more precise measurement of core inflation in the CPI and the greater weight assigned to technology- and consumption-oriented sectors in the IIP. She noted that, for monetary policy, the improvements are expected to yield estimates that are more stable across successive vintages with smaller revisions and reaffirmed RBI’s interest, as a committed user of the data, in a clear and predictable approach to revisions and continued dialogue with MoSPI.
Shri Deepak Parekh,
Former Chairman, HDFC, in his keynote address, drew on more than five decades of experience to underline how macroeconomic numbers move markets, shape investor sentiment and guide decisions of banks, companies and policymakers. Observing that “what gets measured gets managed and what is monitored can be improved”, he said that numbers must reflect reality as it is and that the independence and integrity of statistical institutions, as providers of a public good, must remain sacrosanct. He described 2026 as a year of modernising India’s statistical architecture, noted that the revisions address concerns earlier raised on the national accounts and welcomed the growing use of high-frequency indicators and new data sources such as night lights and online search trends, while cautioning that technology and AI must be supported by appropriate safeguards and cannot substitute for judgement. He also flagged the need for official data on housing statistics, given the sector’s strong backward and forward linkages with allied industries.
The inaugural session was followed by three technical sessions on the new series of GDP, CPI and IIP, in which officers of MoSPI and the RBI presented the methodological changes, data sources and key improvements.
The first technical session, moderated by Prof. Basanta Kumar Pradhan, Director (Vice Chancellor), IGIDR, discussed the new GDP series with base year 2022-23. Shri Rajesh Kumar Sharma, Deputy Director General, National Accounts Division, MoSPI, explained that the revision reflects changes in the structure of the economy, relative prices and consumption patterns, along with new data sources and updated international standards. He elaborated on the key changes, namely the robust and direct annual measurement of the unincorporated sector using ASUSE and PLFS data; the use of MCA-21 filings to allocate corporate GVA across activities; the revised treatment of food subsidies routed through the FCI, government pension contributions and imputed rent on government housing; the introduction of double deflation for constant-price estimation of manufacturing GVA in addition to agriculture; improvements in the estimation of private final consumption expenditure; and an expanded Supply-Use Table integrated with the national accounts. Changes in the compilation of the quarterly national accounts were also presented, including proportional benchmarking, updated price indices and the enhanced use of administrative data from GST, e-VAHAN and PFMS. Users were briefed on the release of the detailed National Accounts Statistics publication on 31 August 2026 and of the ‘Sources and Methods for Compilation of National Accounts Statistics’ document on 21 September 2026. Dr. Anirban Sanyal, Assistant Adviser, RBI, presented RBI’s model-based nowcasting of current-quarter real GDP and non-agricultural GVA growth, drawing on about 120 high-frequency indicators and approaches including the dynamic factor model, machine-learning models and ridge regression, noting that the dynamic factor model performed best.
The second technical session, moderated by Ms. Rajani Sinha, Chief Economist, CareEdge Group, discussed the new CPI series with base year 2024=100. The Price Statistics Division, MoSPI, presented the revision as a significant step towards modernising India’s price statistics and keeping retail inflation measurement aligned with contemporary household consumption patterns and evolving market structures. The revised series uses the Household Consumption Expenditure Survey 2023-24 for deriving expenditure weights and incorporates an updated consumption basket, a revised weighting structure, expanded geographical and market coverage, adoption of the COICOP 2018 classification and improved methodologies for price collection and index compilation. Extensive use of administrative and e-commerce data in the CPI 2024 series was also highlighted. The RBI presented the implications of these changes for inflation measurement and monetary policy.
The The third technical session, moderated by Shri Ravi Shankar, Executive Director, Reserve Bank of India (RBI), focused on the new series of the Index of Industrial Production (IIP) with base year 2022–23, presented by the Economic Statistics Division (ESD), MoSPI. Ms. Ankita Singh, Deputy Director General, MoSPI, delivered a presentation on the revision of the base year from 2011–12 to 2022–23, highlighting the major methodological and coverage-related improvements introduced in the new series.The revised IIP series broadens its coverage by introducing new sectors, namely "Water Supply, Sewerage and Waste Management" and "Gas Supply", and by including minor minerals and rare earth minerals in the Mining and Quarrying sector. In terms of greater disaggregation, the Mining and Quarrying sector now provides three sub-sectoral indices, namely Metallic Minerals, Non-Metallic Minerals and Fuel Minerals. Similarly, the Electricity Index is now disseminated through two sub-indices, distinguishing electricity generation from renewable and non-renewable sources. The sectoral and sub-sectoral weights have been revised using the relevant data from the National Accounts Statistics and the Annual Survey of Industries (ASI) for the base year 2022–23. An important feature of the new series is the provision for substitution of factories that have closed down, discontinued production or changed their product lines, thereby ensuring that the sample remains representative throughout the life of the series. Further, the Output Producer Price Index (Output PPI) is being used for deflation, in line with international recommendations. The compilation of a chain-linked IIP will also be undertaken on a trial basis to assess its feasibility and reliability.
The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) also made a presentation on industrial and corporate sector analysis and data dissemination. The presentation highlighted how corporate-sector data, sourced from listed companies' financial results, audited annual accounts and quarterly surveys, supports monetary policy formulation, facilitates the assessment of demand conditions ahead of GDP releases, and provides insights into private-sector investment and financial stability. The RBI also showcased its Database on Indian Economy (DBIE) and the RBIDATA mobile application, highlighting ongoing initiatives to enhance the timeliness, accessibility and standardisation of economic data.
Each technical session was followed by an open house discussion in which participants offered feedback on the new data sources, methodologies and their implications for policy and forecasting and officials of MoSPI and the RBI responded to the queries raised. In the concluding session, closing remarks were delivered, followed by the vote of thanks by the Deputy Director General, National Accounts Division, MoSPI.
The conference provided a valuable opportunity for data users and official data compilers to directly discuss the changes in the methodologies, their interpretation and implications, and reaffirmed MoSPI’s commitment to promoting better understanding and effective use of official statistics, in line with the vision of “data for development” and Viksit Bharat 2047.

A brief about the coverage, sampling scheme, and data collection mechanism in the Annual Survey of Unincorporated Sector Enterprises
(
ASUSE
):
A
. Coverage
:
A.1. Geographically,
the survey
covers the rural and urban areas of whole of India (except some of the villages in Andaman and Nicobar Islands, which are difficult to access).
A.2. Sector-wise, this survey captures unincorporated non-agricultural establishments belonging to three sectors viz., Manufacturing, Trade and Other Services.
A.3. Ownership-wise, unincorporated non-agricultural establishments pertaining to proprietorship, partnership (excluding Limited Liability Partnerships), co-operatives, societies/trusts etc. have been covered
in this survey
.
B
.
Sampling Scheme
:
The survey has been conducted following a multi
-stage stratified sampling scheme, where first stage units (FSUs) are census villages in rural area (except for rural Keralam, where Panchayat wards have been taken as FSUs) and UFS (Urban Frame Survey) blocks in urban areas
which are updated periodically. The ultimate stage units (USUs) are establishments for both the sectors. In the case of large FSUs, one intermediate stage of sampling has been done in the form of hamlet groups in rural and sub-blocks in urban.
C
.
Sample Size
:
At all-India level, 6,002 First Stage Units (2,411 villages in rural sector and 3,591 UFS blocks in urban sector) have been surveyed during the quarter July, 2026 – September, 2026. This excludes FSUs of Andaman & Nicobar Islands, Lakshadweep, Ladakh and rural areas of Arunachal Pradesh and Nagaland which are not considered for this quarterly bulletin, as sub-round restrictions were not imposed in these areas while conducting field-work, due to arduous field conditions. Accordingly, the number of establishments surveyed (excluding these states/UTs/areas) and considered for this bulletin are 1,80,025 (77,038 in rural and 1,02,987 in urban).
D
.
Data Collection Mechanism
:
The survey has been conducted based on area frame and establishments have been listed in the selected FSUs of both rural and urban sector and from the listed establishments in the FSUs
, requisite number of establishments were surveyed as per the sampling design. Mostly, data were collected from the selected establishments through oral enquiry pertaining to the ‘monthly’ reference period.
The data for the survey were collected in Tablet using Computer Assisted Personal Interviewing (CAPI).
E
.
Comparability of quarterly results with previously released estimates of ASUSE and caveats
:
The estimates presented in this quarterly bulletin pertain specifically to the unincorporated non-agricultural sector for the reference quarter under consideration. The comparison presented in this bulletin is between the quarter under consideration in the current year and the corresponding quarter of the previous year. Such year-on-year comparison accounts for inherent seasonal variations, if any, and facilitates a more meaningful assessment of annual growth trends since the comparison is made between the same periods of two years.
Although sampling design of ASUSE has provision for generation of quarterly estimates using an area frame, the quarterly sample size is significantly less than the annual sample size. Also, the area frame used for rural sector is based on Census 2011. This bulletin has been prepared with due consideration to sample adequacy and reliability of the estimates.
As part of the continuous effort to keep the survey relevant and responsive to stakeholder requirements, a few changes have been introduced in ASUSE 2026. The ICT block of the ASUSE questionnaire has been comprehensively redesigned with more policy-oriented questions to better capture the extent and nature of ICT usage in the sector. Further, ASUSE 2026 has adopted NIC 2025 in place of NIC 2008, which was used in the earlier rounds of ASUSE. Due to this, some activities like maintenance and repair of motor vehicles and maintenance and repair of motor cycles, mopeds, scooters and three wheelers that were considered under trade in NIC 2008 are now being considered under service sector (NIC 2025) and accordingly, all such establishments engaged in these activities are now counted in “other services” in ASUSE 2026.
Accordingly, users may interpret quarterly movements with caution, considering potential sampling variability, and short-term fluctuations in activity levels and changes in classification and questionnaire. It is important to note that ASUSE covers only a part of the non-agricultural economy, namely, the unincorporated segment of the establishments in manufacturing, trade and services (excluding construction). Hence, the trends observed in the quarterly results of the unincorporated sector as presented in QBUSE, may not directly align with the corresponding quarterly GDP estimates which covers the entire economy. Where relevant, the estimates presented in the Quarterly Bulletin are accompanied by confidence intervals to enable informed interpretation of the estimates.

title: MY Bharat - NSS Records Over 73,500 Participations Across the Nation During Week 10 of ‘Nasha Mukt Yuva for Viksit Bharat’ Campaign
subtitle: More than 28,300 individuals take Nasha Mukt pledge; 17,699 youth participate in 366 sporting tournaments
ministry: Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                23 NOV 2026 8:05PM by PIB Delhi
content:
The Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports, through the Directorate of MY Bharat - National Service Scheme, organised Cluster of Block Level Sports Meets and awareness activities during Week 10 of the 100-Week ‘Nasha Mukt Yuva for Viksit Bharat Sankalp Abhiyan’, recording 73,529 total participations across 162
participating
institutions. The activities included 366 sporting tournaments involving 17,699 participants, 200 pledge ceremonies in which 28,360 individuals took the Nasha Mukt Sankalp and 1,006 grassroots activities. Female participants accounted for nearly 49 per cent of the gender-disaggregated entries.
Launched by Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi on August 2, 2026, the campaign is built around four core pillars: Prevent, Protect, Recover and Lead. Week 10 activities were organised under the Month 3 theme, ‘Strong Communities, Healthy Youth (Gram Seva & Sangathan)’, with a focus on promoting fitness, teamwork, community participation and awareness about substance abuse. The programme covered block-level sports grounds, district stadiums, university and college campuses and Gram Panchayat venues, with participation from 162 institutions across the Nation.
Of the 73,529 total participations recorded, 73,436 were gender-disaggregated entries, comprising 37,471 male and 35,965 female participants. A total of 28,360 individuals, including 14,275 male and 14,085 female participants, took the Nasha Mukt Sankalp during 200 oath ceremonies. Meanwhile, 17,699 athletes, including 9,188 male and 8,511 female participants, competed in sporting tournaments. Female participation accounted for 48.1 per cent of sports competitors and 49.7 per cent of oath participants. Dedicated races for Children With Special Needs (CWSN) were also organised by participating units, including GMSSS-46 in Chandigarh.
In terms of regional participation, Bhopal recorded the highest turnout with 10,403 participations, followed by Chennai with 9,175, Bangalore with 8,478, Chandigarh with 7,992 and Delhi with 7,384. Other regions reporting substantial participation included Hyderabad (5,660), Guwahati (5,490), Jaipur (4,681), Pune (4,027), Kolkata (3,752), Lucknow (2,885), Trivandrum (2,251) and Bhubaneswar (1,351).
The Cluster of Block Level Sports Meets brought together university campuses, affiliated colleges, NSS units and local youth clubs. Competitions were organised in Kabaddi, Kho-Kho, Volleyball, Athletics, Football, Badminton, Basketball, Cricket, Tug-of-War, Chess, Carrom and traditional indigenous games such as Pittu, Gilli Danda and Satoliya. Dedicated competitive categories for female athletes were organised across participating centres.
The sporting events were complemented by awareness activities, including street plays, rallies, walkathons, quizzes, declamation contests and poster and essay competitions. A total of 181 awareness kiosks and stalls were set up across 49 kiosk events, engaging 4,441 individuals. These stalls, organised in coordination with local medical authorities and youth organisations, disseminated Information, Education and Communication (IEC) materials on substance abuse risks, counselling services and the National De-Addiction Helpline (14446).
NSS volunteers also staged 142 street plays (Nukkad Nataks), musical performances and slogan-writing sessions, engaging 9,194 youth and spectators. Another 249 activities, including anti-drug rallies, drug-free youth walkathons, declamation contests, quizzes and poster and essay competitions, mobilised 13,835 participants.
To strengthen community engagement, 108 institutions invited Guests of Honour and subject experts from district administrations, police departments, narcotics and civil excise departments, medical institutions, universities, Panchayati Raj institutions and non-governmental organisations. These included District Administrators, Police Superintendents, medical professionals, University Vice-Chancellors, College Principals, Panchayat Sarpanches and recovery advocates associated with Alcoholics Anonymous and partner NGOs.
Youth volunteers also used digital platforms to amplify the campaign's message, uploading 1,137 Instagram reels and more than 1,278 social media posts using the hashtag #
NashaMuktYuva
.

title: MY Bharat Mobilises Over 95,000 Participants Across 36 States/UTs During Week 10 of ‘Nasha Mukt Yuva for Viksit Bharat’ Campaign
subtitle:
440 programmes organised, including 322 Cluster of Blocks Level Sports Meets and 118 Neighbourhood Youth Parliament sessions

Campaign combines grassroots sports, traditional games and youth-led discussions to promote awareness against substance abuse
ministry: Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                23 NOV 2026 8:00PM by PIB Delhi
content:
The tenth week of the 100-week
‘Nasha Mukt Yuva for Viksit Bharat
Abhiyan’
witnessed participation of
95,147
youth and citizens across 36 States and Union Territories through
440
programmes organised by MY Bharat. The activities included 322 Cluster of Blocks Level Sports Meets and 118
‘Nasha Mukt Yuva for Viksit Bharat Par Paricharcha’
(Neighbourhood Youth Parliament) sessions, as per the provisional report dated 22 November 2026.
The Cluster of Blocks Level Sports Meets, organised on 21 and 22 November 2026, brought together youth from multiple blocks and villages for sporting competitions, traditional games and other sports activities. The initiative aimed to promote physical fitness, teamwork, discipline and sportsmanship while connecting grassroots communities with district-level sporting opportunities and providing talented young participants a platform for recognition.
A total of 322 sports programmes were organised, witnessing participation of 81,489 youth and citizens across 1,053 activities. Prominent participation was reported from Uttarakhand, Ernakulam in Kerala, Tirap and Kra Daadi in Arunachal Pradesh, Shopian and Samba in Jammu and Kashmir and Gopalganj in Bihar.
Alongside the sporting activities, ‘Nasha Mukt Yuva for Viksit Bharat Par Paricharcha’ (Neighbourhood Youth Parliament) sessions were organised at the block level on 21 November 2026. With a minimum participation target of 80 youth per block, each NYP featured four structured sessions covering an introduction to the MY Bharat Portal; Understanding Substance Abuse: Challenges before India’s Youth; From Awareness to Action: Tools for a Nasha Mukt Yuva; and an audio-visual presentation on Stories of Change: The Journey Towards a Nasha Mukt Bharat.
The 118 Neighbourhood Youth Parliament programmes recorded participation of 13,658 youth across 360 activities. The sessions provided a platform for young people to discuss the challenges posed by substance abuse, preventive measures and their role in promoting a drug-free society.
Partner organisations, including Brahma Kumaris and Heartfulness, supported the campaign activities. Heartfulness also extended support to sporting events, including badminton competitions organised at Pune.
The campaign also witnessed collaborations at the local level. MY Bharat Meerut organised a Neighbourhood Youth Parliament at Shobhit University, Meerut, in the presence of Dr. Laxmikant Bajpayee, Member of Parliament, Rajya Sabha. In Kupwara, MY Bharat, in coordination with the Indian Army, Keran Bowl and Khatana Action Club, jointly organised a session at Kundian in Keran Block. Other notable initiatives included programmes at Chaibasa Engineering College in Jhinkpani Block, Jharkhand, and Garudeshwar in Narmada district, Gujarat.
By bringing together grassroots sporting competitions and structured youth-led discussions, MY Bharat is combining community participation with awareness-building efforts to promote healthy lifestyles and strengthen the campaign against substance abuse.

title: MY Bharat to organise Yuva Samvad  on Constitution Day; Programme to cover over 600 districts across 30+ States/UTs under the theme ‘Viksit Bharat@2047’
subtitle: Nationwide Student Engagement to Highlight India’s Achievements, Constitutional Values and the Role of Youth in Nation-Building; Participants to collectively read the Preamble to the Constitution
ministry: Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                23 NOV 2026 1:00PM by PIB Delhi
content:
The
Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports
, through
Mera Yuva Bharat (MY Bharat)
, will organise the
‘Viksit Bharat Yuva Samvad’
on the occasion of
Constitution Day, between 24th and 26th November 2026
, across more than
500 colleges in over 600 districts spanning 30+ States and Union Territories
. The nationwide initiative aims to connect young people in the age group of
15–29 years
with India's developmental journey, its achievements and aspirations for the future, while inspiring them to become active participants in the nation's transformation into a developed country by 2047.
In keeping with the spirit of Constitution Day, participants across institutions will collectively undertake a
reading of the Preamble to the Constitution of India
, reaffirming their commitment to constitutional values and the ideals enshrined in the Constitution. The programme will also provide a nationwide platform for engaging young people through
interactive dialogues and awareness sessions
, encouraging them to reflect on India's progress, emerging opportunities and their role in shaping the country's future.
To translate this vision into meaningful engagement at the grassroots level, distinguished
Youth Icons
will lead sessions at participating universities and colleges. As a key component of these engagements, each Youth Icon will deliver a specially curated presentation on the theme
‘Viksit Bharat@2047’
, taking students through India's developmental journey, its achievements in recent years and its aspirations for becoming a developed nation by 2047. The presentation will highlight the country's progress in
poverty reduction and socio-economic transformation
, including efforts to improve the lives and livelihood opportunities of millions of people through inclusive development and welfare initiatives. It will also showcase India's significant progress in addressing
Naxalism
, restoring peace and creating an enabling environment for development in previously affected regions. Further, it will emphasise the importance of building a healthy, empowered and addiction-free society, highlighting how substance abuse undermines individual potential, family well-being, societal progress and national productivity. The presentation will underline that
a Nasha Mukt Bharat is fundamental to realising the vision of Viksit Bharat@2047
, with the youth playing a decisive role in driving this transformation.
Adding further depth to these interactions,
Padma Awardees
will engage with students and share their life journeys, personal experiences and insights, highlighting the challenges they have overcome, the milestones they have achieved and the values that have guided their journeys. These interactions will provide young participants with an opportunity to draw inspiration from their experiences and understand the importance of dedication, perseverance and commitment in contributing to nation-building.
The initiative draws inspiration from the vision of
Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi
, articulated in his address on
15th August 2023 from the ramparts of the Red Fort
, wherein he called upon the
Yuva Shakti
to play a pivotal role in realising
Viksit Bharat@2047
. Recognising the
Amrit Peedhi
as a key driver of nation-building, the programme seeks to channelise youth energy and leadership towards achieving this national vision.
To translate the vision of Viksit Bharat@2047 into action,  the
MY Bharat Portal (
mybharat.gov.in
)
will serve as the digital platform for registrations and programme-related activities, enabling wider youth participation and facilitating the onboarding of young people into the MY Bharat ecosystem. By combining institutional outreach with digital engagement, the initiative seeks to extend opportunities for participation to youth across the country and encourage them to take up meaningful volunteer-led activities.
The programme will also establish a sustained institutional connection with participating colleges and universities.
MY Bharat Chapters may subsequently be established in these institutions
to facilitate continued youth engagement, promote volunteerism and support the implementation of future MY Bharat initiatives. This will help nurture a network of socially responsible and motivated young citizens who can take forward the spirit of participation, leadership and service beyond the programme.
Through the
‘Viksit Bharat Yuva Samvad’
, MY Bharat seeks to channelise the
energy, ideas and potential of the Amrit Peedhi
towards the national vision of
Viksit Bharat@2047
. India's journey towards becoming a developed nation is rooted in inclusive growth, social transformation, peace and security, and the empowerment of its citizens. A drug-free India is not merely a social aspiration; it is a national imperative that calls for the active participation of every young citizen.
With the message ‘Nasha Mukt Yuva for Viksit Bharat’, the programme aims to transform awareness into action, dialogue into determination and youth participation into a nationwide movement for change.
This Constitution Day, MY Bharat invites the youth of India to come together for a collective reading of the Preamble, reaffirm their commitment to the ideals enshrined in the Constitution, and raise their voices for a healthier, stronger and drug-free Bharat. The journey towards Viksit Bharat@2047 will be shaped not only by the aspirations of our youth, but also by the choices they make and the actions they take today.
For registrations, programme updates and opportunities to engage with MY Bharat initiatives, visit
www.mybharat.gov.in
.

title: Blooming Beyond Borders
subtitle: “The Rise of India’s Floriculture Economy”
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                23 NOV 2026 1:43PM by PIB Delhi
content:
Roots of a Blooming Industry
India is a land of remarkable natural diversity, stretching from snow-bound mountains and fertile plains to arid deserts and long coastlines. These varied agro-climatic conditions support the cultivation of an extraordinary
variety of flowers
that bloom across regions and seasons. Coupled with the deep cultural, spiritual, and emotional significance of flowers in India, these natural advantages have fostered a thriving floriculture sector.
Recognising its economic and aesthetic potential, the government has identified
floriculture
as a
“
sunrise industry
”
. What was once a relatively niche segment within Indian agriculture has evolved into a dynamic component of the
horticulture
sector. The sector contributes to farmer incomes, agricultural exports, and rural enterprise development while increasingly adopting modern cultivation practices and technologies. Today, floriculture encompasses a diverse range of products, production systems, and value-added applications. Rising consumer demand, widening market opportunities, policy support, and technological advancements are driving its continued growth.
Inside India’s Floral Economy
Floriculture is the art and science of growing flowers to achieve high standards of flower quality and aesthetic appeal. As an integral branch of horticulture, it includes the cultivation of flowers and ornamental crops from
planting to harvesting
. The sector also involves the production of planting material through seeds, cuttings, budding, and grafting. It further includes the marketing of flowers and flower-based products.
Floriculture Product Categories
Loose flowers
are harvested and marketed without long stems. These are generally sold by weight and are commonly used for garlands and
gajras
. Examples include
marigolds and jasmine.
Retail Shop selling loose flowers as Garlands
Cut Flowers
are harvested and marketed with stems. These are commonly used in bouquets and vase arrangements. Examples include
roses, gerberas, carnations, orchids, and lilies.
Cut flowers sold in bunches as bouquets
In addition to flowers, floriculture includes
cut foliage, potted and bedding plants, and ornamental planting materials
like seeds for propagation and landscaping.
Flowers that Shape the Market
India cultivates a variety of flowers tailored to domestic and international demand. Key varieties include:
Roses:
Widely grown in
Karnataka and Maharashtra
; high in export value.
Marigolds:
Popular in religious ceremonies; extensively grown in
Tamil Nadu and Madhya Pradesh.
Carnations, Chrysanthemums, Gerberas:
Grown in controlled environments for export.
Lilies and Orchids:
High-end flowers grown in select regions like
Sikkim and Mizoram
.
The demand for exotic flowers has increased, with
orchids and anthuriums
becoming commercially viable in the
north-eastern region
. These flowers are also gaining traction in urban landscaping, event decor, and the wellness industry.
From Open Fields to Protected Farms
Cultivation of flowers in India takes place through both open-field and protected systems like greenhouses, depending on crop requirements.
Open-field cultivation
is commonly used for crops such as
Chrysanthemum, Rose, Gaillardia, Lily, Marigold, Aster, and Tuberose
.
Rising demand for quality flowers and year-round availability have encouraged greater adoption of
protected cultivation such as greenhouses
.
Greenhouses
are particularly important for export-oriented crops such as
Gerberas and Carnations
. This ensures better control over temperature, humidity, and other growing conditions. This helps ensure uniform quality, improved productivity, and compliance with international market standards.
Beyond Bouquets: The Many Uses of Floriculture
Flowers play an important role in everyday life in India and are closely linked with cultural, social, and religious practices. Beyond these traditional uses, floriculture has evolved into a diversified sector with expanding applications in perfumery, cosmetics, and pharmaceuticals.
Key domestic uses:
Religious and social practices
- Flowers such as
Jasmine, Marigold, and Crossandra
are commonly used in worship, social ceremonies, and personal decoration.
Lifestyle and decorative uses
- Increasing urbanisation and rising disposable incomes have driven demand for bouquet gifting, venue decoration and beautification of residential and commercial spaces.
Perfumery and cosmetics
- Flowers, including
Jasmine, Lavender, and Rose petals,
are used as raw material in fragrance and cosmetic products.
Pharmaceutical applications
- Floricultural crops such as
Calendula, Hibiscus, and Chamomile
are utilised in pharmaceutical preparations.
Dye and colour extraction
-
Marigold and Hibiscus
are used for natural dyeing and colour extraction.
Mapping India's Flower Belt
Supported by favourable climatic conditions and expanding market demand, floriculture cultivation has expanded across several regions of the country. According to the Third Advance Estimates for 2025-26, the total area under floriculture cultivation stood at
410 thousand hectares.
During the same period, production included
3,653 thousand metric tonnes of loose flowers
and
1,229 thousand metric tonnes of cut flowers.
Total floriculture output amounted to
4,882 thousand metric tonnes,
reflecting the scale and commercial significance of floriculture cultivation in India.
The States Driving Floral Production
Floriculture production in India is concentrated in a few leading states.  According to the Third Advance Estimates for 2025-26,
Andhra Pradesh
accounted for about
31 percent
of the country’s total flower production. It is followed by
Tamil Nadu (14 percent)
,
Madhya Pradesh (11 percent),
Karnataka (10 percent),
and
West Bengal (8 percent)
. Other major producers included
Chhattisgarh, Gujarat, Uttar Pradesh,
Maharashtra,
Odisha and Telangana.
The Northeastern states together accounted for about
4 percent
of India’s total flower production, with
Assam
contributing substantially through both
loose and cut flowers.
This was followed by
Nagaland
, particularly in cut flowers. This distribution reflects the diverse geographical spread of floriculture across the country.
A strong production base and diversified cultivation systems have also supported India's growing presence in the international flower trade.
India's Growing Footprint in Global Flower Markets
Floriculture forms part of value-added agricultural exports and provides additional income opportunities beyond traditional crop cultivation. India’s floriculture exports have followed a clear upward trend over the past few years, signalling increasing international demand for Indian floral products. Exports of floriculture, including fruits and vegetable seeds, rose from
USD 216.74 million
in
FY 2021-22
to
USD 258.26 million
in
FY 2025-26
. This growth reflects rising international demand for Indian floral products and strengthening export competitiveness.
India’s Top Global Destinations
In
FY 2025-26
, India’s floriculture and seeds recorded strong demand across key international markets. The
United States
emerged as the top destination, with exports worth
USD 45.94 million
. It was followed by the
Netherlands
, a significant base of the international flower trade, with
USD 42.18 million
.
Bangladesh
accounted for floriculture imports worth
USD 16.51 million
. The
United Arab Emirates
and
Italy
imported products valued at
USD 16.35 million
and
USD 9.69 million
, respectively. This highlights India’s expanding footprint in traditional and emerging markets for floriculture exports.
A Diverse Floral Export Portfolio
This export performance is supported by a diverse range of floricultural crops that are commercially relevant in the global cut flower trade. Prominent export crops from India include
Rose, Carnation, Chrysanthemum, Gerbera, Gladiolus, Gypsophila, Liatris, Nerine, Orchids, Achillea, Anthurium, Tulip, and Lilies
, enabling the country to cater to varied market preferences and quality requirements worldwide.
Further, floriculture exports from India comprise multiple product categories, each catering to specific international markets:
Fresh cut flowers
are exported mainly to
Europe, Japan, Australia, the Middle East, and the United States of America
Loose flowers
are supplied largely to markets serving
expatriate Indian communities in the Gulf region
Cut foliage
is exported primarily to
European countries
Dry flowers
are exported to a wide range of destinations, including the
United States of America, Europe, Japan, Australia, the Far East, and Russia
Potted plants
are exported to a limited number of countries.
Among these export segments,
dry flowers constitute a major share of India’s total floriculture exports
, owing to their longer shelf life and wider market reach.
Export Breakthrough from the North East
In
February 2025
, the
first-ever export consignment of Anthurium flowers from Mizoram to Singapore
was flagged off. This marked a significant milestone for floriculture exports from
India’s North Eastern Region.
The consignment contained
1,024 Anthurium cut flowers
(weighing 70 kg) packed in 50 corrugated boxes. The initiative was led by
APEDA
in collaboration with the
Department of Horticulture, Government of Mizoram
. It highlights new overseas market linkages and emerging trade opportunities for floriculture growers in the region.
Enabling Growth Through Policy Support
The government has initiated a range of developmental programmes to promote floriculture across the country. These efforts focus on production, infrastructure, research, capacity building, and export facilitation.
Key areas of government support include:
Policy and Institutional Support
- Developmental initiatives are implemented primarily through the
Mission for Integrated Development of Horticulture (MIDH)
, including the
National Horticulture Mission (NHM), the Horticulture Mission for North East and Himalayan States, and the National Horticulture Board
.
Financial assistance and credit support
-
The National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development (NABARD)
provides financial assistance to farmers to adopt
protected cultivation and precision farming
practices, thereby improving productivity and quality.
Seed production and planting material
- To meet growing demand for flower seeds, several seed companies have established production units in major flower-growing states. Thus, supporting the availability of quality planting material.
Incentives and concessions
- Concessions are provided on
seeds, planting materials, equipment, and air freight
to support floriculture exports and improve competitiveness in international markets.
Export Promotion
- Export-related support is provided through the
Ministry of Commerce, mainly via
the
Agricultural and Processed Food Products Export Development Authority (APEDA).
Training and capacity building
- The Government has introduced various
training programmes for farmers and entrepreneurs
. These programmes are strengthening farmers’ technical skills, promoting the adoption of modern practices, and enterprise development in floriculture.
Research and development
- Floriculture research is carried out at multiple institutions under the
Indian Council of Agricultural Research (ICAR)
and the
Council of Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR)
. The research is also conducted in the horticulture departments of
State Agricultural Universities
, and under the
All India Coordinated Floriculture Improvement Project
.
The sector continues to benefit from policy support, financial assistance, and institutional backing. Improved frameworks and targeted interventions will further enhance India's competitiveness in the floriculture trade.
Cultivating Innovation: From Scientific Research to High-Value Floriculture
As floriculture becomes increasingly market-oriented, advances in research and technology are improving productivity, quality, and product diversification.
CSIR Floriculture Mission
The
Council of Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR)
has developed two flagship programmes to strengthen India’s
flower and aroma sectors
through science-driven interventions.
The CSIR Floriculture Mission
, launched in 2021, seeks to enhance farmers’ incomes, support entrepreneurship, and promote technology-led development in the floriculture industry.
As of December 2025, under this mission, more than
2,208 hectares
have been brought under floricultural cultivation.
This has benefitted
16,220 individuals across 399 clusters
in
26 states and union territories
of the country.
The programme has also developed and transferred multiple technologies to entrepreneurs and conducted numerous training and capacity-building initiatives.
The CSIR Aroma Mission
, launched in
2017
, focuses on improving rural livelihoods through the cultivation and processing of aromatic crops
.
Thesecrops provide quality raw materials for the aroma and essential oil industry.
As of December 2025, aromatic crop cultivation had expanded to
more than 51,000 hectares.
The mission had also established
over 4,500 aroma clusters across 28 States
, including
20 clusters in tribal areas
.
The mission prioritised skill development, with
2,096 training and awareness programmes
training
1.22 lakh persons
. These included
10,000 women
and supported more than
110 entrepreneurs
in developing value-added products.
In total, these interventions have generated around
1 crore rural employment opportunities
and enabled the production of
over 6,000 tonnes of essential oils
. The output valued at about
Rs.
600 crore
supplied key inputs to the aroma and allied industries.
These research initiatives highlight the importance of scientific support in strengthening India's floriculture sector.
From Laboratory to Field: The Story of India’s Exotic Flowers
Tulips in the Himalayas: A Garden of Possibilities
In the
Himalayan region (Palampur),
scientific research under the
CSIR - Institute of Himalayan Bioresource Technology (IHBT)
-Floriculture Mission, has helped convert natural climatic advantage into structured floriculture opportunity. Leveraging cool temperatures and suitable agro-ecological conditions, tulip cultivation has been supported through research-driven interventions. The work has focussed on
planting material selection, flowering cycles and crop management practices
. These efforts have enabled the successful growth of tulips meeting international quality parameters. They have also strengthened the region’s position in premium ornamental flower segments. As of May 2026, the Tulip Garden at Palampur attracted more than 1.5 lakh visitors, highlighting its potential to support floriculture-based tourism.
The Himalayan tulip initiative demonstrates how targeted technological interventions can support crop diversification. It also highlights the potential for strengthening regional specialisation in high-value floriculture.
Tulip Garden at CSIR-IHBT Palampur, Himachal Pradesh
Eustoma in Odisha: A New Bloom of Hope
In contrast to the cool Himalayan landscape, another
CSIR
laboratory has created floral history. The successful cultivation of
Eustoma
in parts of
Odisha (Sambalpur)
represents a breakthrough in adapting exotic flowers to non-traditional environments. Once considered unsuitable for warmer regions, the crop was grown with scientific guidance on temperature management, disease control and cultivation practices. The outcome demonstrated that
innovation can overcome climatic constraints, opening new income avenues for farmers.
The Odisha experience highlight show
science-led cultivation
can connect farmers with
high-value markets
.
First Bloom of Eustoma in Odisha
For visitors walking through the tulip fields of Palampur or admiring the pastel blooms of Eustoma in Sambalpur, the experience extends beyond visual appeal. It represents the quiet yet impactful transformation of laboratory knowledge into practical field-level success. Here, innovation takes root and strengthens India's evolving floriculture landscape.
A Sector Poised for Sustainable Growth
India’s floriculture sector has moved beyond a niche segment of horticulture to become a
diversified and commercially significant agricultural activity
. Its growth is anchored in the country’s rich agro-climatic diversity, expanding domestic demand, stronger market linkages, and growing export opportunities. The sector’s future lies in moving
from cultivation to value creation
. Greater adoption of protected cultivation, precision technologies, improved planting material, post-harvest management, and quality standards can strengthen productivity and market competitiveness. With continued policy support, stronger institutions, and better market linkages, floriculture can boost
farm incomes, rural enterprises, and agricultural exports
.
The sector’s expanding footprint, from
traditional flowers to exotic varieties
and value-added applications, also opens avenues for regional specialization and new entrepreneurial opportunities. As India looks towards a more diversified and technology-enabled agricultural economy,
the future of floriculture holds the promise of growing both value and livelihoods
- “one bloom at a time”.
